docs.title: From voltage to number: the ADC
docs.text:
Try simulation: ADC

  • Many sensors produce a voltage that tells how much: light, temperature, position, humidity.

  • The ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) turns that voltage into a number.

  • ESP32: 12 bits \(\Rightarrow\) \(2^{12} = 4096\) steps: 0 V \(\rightarrow\) 0 … 3.3 V \(\rightarrow\) 4095.

  • One step (LSB) \(\approx 3.3 / 4095 \approx 0.8\) mV. (The drawing uses only 3 bits = 8 steps.)

Formula

\(V = \text{raw} \times \dfrac{3.3}{4095}\) raw \(= V \times \dfrac{4095}{3.3}\)

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation; Espressif: GPIO Matrix and Pin Mux

docs.title: Sampling: reading a changing signal
docs.text:
Try simulation: ADC

  • Every analogRead() is one sample: a snapshot of the voltage at that moment.

  • The resolution (bits) sets the vertical precision.

  • The sample rate (samples per second) sets how fast changes can be followed.

Aliasing

Sample at least 2\(\times\) faster than the fastest change (Nyquist).

Sources: Figures: lecture 2 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Connecting a potentiometer
docs.text:
Try simulation: ADC

  • A potentiometer is a resistor track with a sliding contact (the wiper): a voltage divider you turn by hand.

  • Outer pins: one to 3V3, the other to GND. Middle pin (wiper) to an ADC pin.

  • Turning the knob moves the wiper voltage from 0 V to 3.3 V.

  • Course board: outer pins on the 3V3/GND terminal, wiper on the AD1 terminal (GPIO36). Breadboard: any ADC1 pin (32–39).

  • Typical value: 10 k\(\Omega\) (anything 1–100 k\(\Omega\) works).

Common wiring mistakes

5 V / VIN on the pot: input above 3.3 V. Wiper to 3V3: at the end position the pot shorts 3V3 to GND. Outer pins on the same rail: the value never changes. Outer pins swapped: direction reversed (harmless).

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: From ADC value to voltage, step by step
docs.text:
Try simulation: ADC

The steps

  1. analogRead(36) measures the wiper voltage and returns a number 0 … 4095 (12 bits).

  2. 0 means 0 V, 4095 means (about) 3.3 V: the relation is linear.

  3. Convert: \(V = \text{raw} \times \dfrac{3.3}{4095}\)

  4. Percentage of the knob: \(\% = \text{raw} \times \dfrac{100}{4095}\)

Use 4095.0

raw * 3.3 / 4095.0 is correct. With raw / 4095 * 3.3 the integer division gives 0 for every raw value below 4095.

Worked examples

raw voltage knob 0 0.00 V 0 % 1024 0.83 V 25 % 2048 1.65 V 50 % 3071 2.47 V 75 % 4095 3.30 V 100 %

Example: raw \(= 2048\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(2048 \times 3.3 / 4095 = 1.650\) V

Real ESP32

The ESP32 ADC is not perfectly linear: analogReadMilliVolts() applies the factory calibration (following sections).

docs.title: Code: read the potentiometer and convert to volts
docs.text:
Try simulation: ADC

pot_voltage.ino
const int POT_PIN = 36;            // AD1 terminal (wiper)
const float VREF = 3.3;            // full-scale voltage
const int ADC_MAX = 4095;          // 12-bit ADC
float toVolts(int raw) {
  return raw * VREF / ADC_MAX;     // float result
}
int toPercent(int raw) {
  return raw * 100L / ADC_MAX;     // 100L: no overflow
}
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
}
void loop() {
  int raw = analogRead(POT_PIN);
  float volts = toVolts(raw);
  int mv = analogReadMilliVolts(POT_PIN);  // calibrated
  Serial.printf("raw:%d,volts:%.2f,mV:%d,percent:%d\n",
                raw, volts, mv, toPercent(raw));
  delay(100);
}

Download this example

  1. Upload, open the Serial Monitor (115200) and turn the knob from end to end.

  2. Check: raw goes 0 \(\rightarrow\) 4095, volts 0.00 \(\rightarrow\) 3.30.

  3. Open the Serial Plotter: the labels become four lines.

  4. Compare volts with mV and with a multimeter on the wiper.

What you will see

Near the ends the calculated volts and the calibrated mV differ: that is the ADC non-linearity.

docs.title: Analog input: the 12-bit ADC
docs.text:
Try simulation: ADC

adc.ino
const int POT_PIN = 36;    // AD1 terminal: ADC1, OK with Wi-Fi

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  analogReadResolution(12);         // 0..4095 (default)
  analogSetAttenuation(ADC_11db);   // range ~0..3.1 V
}

void loop() {
  int raw = analogRead(POT_PIN);
  int mv  = analogReadMilliVolts(POT_PIN); // calibrated
  Serial.printf("raw=%4d  voltage=%4d mV\n", raw, mv);
  delay(200);
}

Download this example

  • \(V \approx \text{raw} \cdot 3.3 / 4095\), but the ADC is non-linear: prefer analogReadMilliVolts().

  • Use Serial Plotter to see the signal.

  • Noisy? Average \(N\) samples.

Sources: Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation; Espressif: GPIO Matrix and Pin Mux

docs.title: The ESP32 ADC is not perfect
docs.text:
Attenuation Accurate input range ADC_0db 100 – 950 mV ADC_2_5db 100 – 1250 mV ADC_6db 150 – 1750 mV ADC_11db (default) 150 – 2450 mV

  • Non-linear near 0 V and above \(\approx\) 2.5 V.

  • Noisy: average several samples.

  • ADC2 does not work while Wi-Fi is on.

Copying Arduino Uno code

float v = raw * 5.0 / 1023.0; is for a 10-bit, 5 V Uno. On the ESP32: raw * 3.3 / 4095.0, or better analogReadMilliVolts(pin), which uses the factory calibration.

Change resolution

analogReadResolution(10); gives 0–1023 like an Uno; analogSetAttenuation() or analogSetPinAttenuation() changes the range.

Sources: Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation; ESP32 Series Datasheet

docs.title: Measuring higher voltages: the voltage divider
docs.text:
• Two resistors divide the voltage: \(V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 5 \cdot \dfrac{20}{30} = 3.33\) V

  • In code, multiply back: \(V_{in} = V_{out} \cdot \dfrac{R_1 + R_2}{R_2} = V_{out} \times 1.5\)

  • Use for: batteries, 5 V sensors, solar panels.

  • Choose \(R_1 + R_2\) in the 10–100 k\(\Omega\) range: small current, still fast enough for the ADC.

A potentiometer is a voltage divider

The wiper moves the point between \(R_1\) and \(R_2\): 0 V at one end, 3.3 V at the other.

docs.title: Example: light sensor with map() and constrain()
PWM: faking an analog output
docs.text:
• Pulse Width Modulation: switch the pin on and off very fast.

  • Duty cycle = time on / period.

  • The average voltage = duty \(\times\) 3.3 V.

  • LEDs and motors respond to the average: smooth dimming, speed control.

  • Frequency high enough that you do not see flicker (\(>\) 200 Hz for LEDs).

Simplest way

analogWrite(pin, 0..255); works on the ESP32 core 3.x (it uses the LEDC peripheral underneath).

docs.title: Quiz: analog and PWM
docs.text:
1. analogRead() returns 2048. What is the voltage (ideal ADC)?

    Check your answer

    \(2048 \times 3.3 / 4095 \approx 1.65\) V.

  2. How many levels does a 10-bit ADC have? And a 12-bit one?

    Check your answer

    1024 and 4096.

  3. 8-bit PWM, value 64: what is the duty cycle and average voltage?

    Check your answer

    \(64/255 \approx 25\,\%\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\approx\) 0.83 V.

  4. A 5 V sensor output must be read. Design a divider.

    Check your answer

    E.g. \(R_1\) = 10 k\(\Omega\), \(R_2\) = 20 k\(\Omega\) \(\Rightarrow\) max 3.33 V.

  5. Why does the pot only reach “full brightness” at half-turn?

    Check your answer

    Human vision is logarithmic; use a gamma curve.

docs.title: What is a microcontroller?
docs.text:
• A complete small computer on one chip: processor, memory, input/output and clock.

  • Built to control something: read sensors, drive actuators, communicate.

  • No screen, keyboard or operating system needed: it runs one program, directly on the hardware.

  • Found everywhere: washing machines, cars (50–100 per car), toys, thermostats.

PC vs microcontroller

PC: GHz, gigabytes, many programs. MCU: MHz, kilobytes, one job, milliwatts, starts in milliseconds.

docs.title: The CPU: fetch, decode, execute
docs.text:
1. Fetch the next instruction from memory.

  2. Decode: what operation, which registers?

  3. Execute: add, compare, load, store, jump…

  4. 240 MHz = 240 million clock ticks per second; simple instructions take 1 tick.

  5. One line of C may become several instructions.

  6. 32-bit CPU: works on 32-bit numbers in one step.

How fast is fast?

A digitalWrite() takes about 0.1 μs; a delay(1) wastes \(\approx\) 240 000 clock ticks.

docs.title: CPU and memory
docs.text:
Two Xtensa LX6 cores

  • PRO_CPU (core 0): Wi-Fi / BT stacks and system tasks.

  • APP_CPU (core 1): runs setup() and loop() in Arduino.

  • Up to 240 MHz (also 160 / 80 MHz to save power), 600 DMIPS.

  • ULP co-processor: tiny core that runs while the main CPUs sleep.

Memory

  • 448 KB ROM: boot loader + core functions.

  • 520 KB SRAM (data + instructions).

  • 16 KB RTC memory: survives deep sleep (RTC_DATA_ATTR).

  • External SPI flash (4 MB in WROOM-32), executed through a cache (XIP).

  • Optional PSRAM (WROVER modules).

  • 1 Kbit eFuse: MAC address, keys, chip config.

Sources: ESP32 Series Datasheet; ESP32 Technical Reference Manual

docs.title: Memory types: capacity, purpose and retention
docs.text:
The course board uses several memories for different jobs.

@L1.7cmL2.1cmL5.5cmL2.7cm@ **Memory** & **Capacity here** & **What it is for** & **Keeps data?** ROM & 448 KB & Factory boot code and built-in routines; not rewritten by your sketch. & Without power: yes Internal SRAM & 520 KB total & Fast working memory for program data and some instructions. & Without power: no SPI flash & 4 MB on module & Uploaded firmware, stored settings and files; electrically rewritable. & Without power: yes RTC SRAM & 8 KB FAST + 8 KB SLOW & Small retained data/code areas for low-power operation. & In deep sleep, if powered PSRAM & None on WROOM-32 & Optional extra external RAM on other modules, such as WROVER. & Without power: no eFuse & 1 Kbit (128 bytes) & One-time programmable identity/configuration bits; partly reserved. & Without power: yes

Chip SRAM, module flash and free heap are different quantities; only part of SRAM is free for your application.

Sources: Classic ESP32 and WROOM-32 capacities ESP32 Series Datasheet; ESP32-WROOM-32 Datasheet, Version 3.8

docs.title: Inside RAM: globals, stack, heap and instructions
docs.text:
Different uses of the same working memory

  • Global/static data: exists for the entire run; not recreated on every function call.

  • Stack: function calls and ordinary local variables; automatically reclaimed on return.

  • Heap: dynamically allocated buffers and objects, including storage used by String.

ESP32 names you will encounter

  • DRAM means Data RAM in ESP32 documentation: RAM used for data.

  • IRAM means Instruction RAM: RAM used for executable code, including suitably placed ISRs.

  • These are uses/mappings of internal SRAM, not extra 520 KB memories.

Why less memory is free than the headline capacity

The program, caches, buffers and system libraries already occupy memory. A large local array uses stack space; a large dynamic buffer consumes heap. Neither increases the physical RAM capacity.

Sources: Memory allocation and IRAM/DRAM terminology ESP-IDF Programming Guide: Memory Types (ESP32)

docs.title: Which memory should hold this value?
docs.text:
@L4.2cmL3.1cmL4.4cm@ **Example** & **Use** & **Reason** Current temperature, state, timer & Ordinary RAM variables & Changes during execution Threshold saved by the user & `Preferences` / NVS in flash & Must survive restart and power loss HTML page or log file & Flash filesystem, e.g. LittleFS & Data organised as files Counter retained in deep sleep & RTC RAM, e.g. `RTC_DATA_ATTR` & Retention while the RTC domain stays powered Large image/audio buffer & PSRAM, if the module has it & More volatile working storage

NVS, filesystems and EEPROM are not extra memory chips

NVS and LittleFS share the flash capacity. The classic ESP32 has no separate EEPROM block: use Preferences for small persistent settings. Save settings when they change, not on every loop.

Sources: Memory types and persistent storage ESP-IDF Programming Guide: Memory Types (ESP32); Arduino ESP32: Preferences Library

Try simulation: Memory layout

Analogy

Flash is the book on the shelf; RAM is the notepad on your desk: fast, but wiped when you leave.

docs.title: Peripherals: hardware that works for you
docs.text:
• A peripheral is a dedicated hardware block next to the CPU: UART, I2C, SPI, PWM, ADC, timers …

  • The CPU only configures it; the peripheral then runs in parallel.

  • Example: a PWM channel keeps an LED dimmed while your code does something else.

  • Peripherals signal events to the CPU with interrupts.

GPIO matrix

On the ESP32 most peripheral signals can be routed to almost any GPIO. That is why Serial2.begin(115200, SERIAL_8N1, 16, 17); lets you choose the pins.

Software vs hardware

“Bit-banging” (toggling pins in code) works, but costs CPU time and is less precise than a peripheral.

Sources: ESP32 Technical Reference Manual

docs.title: Power modes
docs.text:
• Log scale: 5 orders of magnitude between transmitting and hibernating.

  • Battery products spend most of their life in deep sleep.

  • Modem-sleep: CPU on, radio off between DTIM beacons.

  • Wake sources: timer, GPIO (ext0/ext1), touch, ULP.

Sources: Typical values, ESP32 Series Datasheet ESP32 Series Datasheet; ESP-IDF Programming Guide: Sleep Modes (ESP32)

docs.title: Inside the DevKit V1 board
docs.text:
• Module: ESP32 chip + 40 MHz crystal + 4 MB flash + PCB antenna under a shield.

  • USB–UART bridge (CP2102 or CH340): programming + Serial.

  • LDO: 5 V (USB / VIN) \(\rightarrow\) 3.3 V.

  • EN: reset button. BOOT: holds GPIO0 LOW \(\rightarrow\) download mode.

  • On-board LED on GPIO2.

Sources: ESP32-WROOM-32E & ESP32-WROOM-32UE Datasheet; ESP32 Hardware Design Guidelines

docs.title: Quiz: architecture
docs.text:
1. Your program survives a power cycle, but a counter variable restarts at 0. Why?

    Check your answer

    The program is in flash (non-volatile); variables live in SRAM (volatile).

  2. Which core runs setup() and loop() in the Arduino core?

    Check your answer

    Core 1 (APP_CPU); core 0 handles the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth stacks.

  3. How many clock cycles does the CPU run during delay(10) at 240 MHz?

    Check your answer

    \(240 \cdot 10^6 \times 0.010 = 2.4\) million cycles, all wasted waiting.

  4. Name two advantages of a hardware peripheral over bit-banging.

    Check your answer

    Runs in parallel with your code, precise timing, lower CPU load.

docs.title: From sketch to running firmware
docs.text:
Sketch structure

setup() runs once after reset; loop() runs forever. Everything in loop() repeats as fast as possible: thousands of times per second.

“Connecting…_____” never ends?

Hold BOOT when “Connecting” appears, release when writing starts. Disconnect anything on GPIO 0, 2, 12.

docs.title: The structure of every sketch
docs.text:
• void setup() runs once after power-up or reset: initialisation (pin modes, Serial, sensors).

  • void loop() runs again and again, for as long as the board has power.

  • Statements inside the braces { } run top to bottom, one after the other.

  • Code outside both functions: global variables, constants, #include, your own functions.

  • void means: the function returns nothing.

There is no “end”

An embedded program never finishes. When loop() reaches its last line, it simply starts again at the top.

Sources: Arduino Language Reference; Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

The Serial Monitor and the Serial Plotter
docs.text:
Serial Monitor (magnifier icon, top right)

  • Shows the text your sketch prints with Serial.print().

  • The baud rate in the monitor must match Serial.begin(115200).

  • You can also send text to the board (input line at the top).

  • Choose the line ending: Newline is easiest for commands.

Serial Plotter (graph icon)

  • Draws numbers as live graphs.

  • One value per line, or several separated by commas: Serial.printf("pot:%d,light:%d\ n", a, b);

  • Labels before the colon become the legend.

  • Only one of the two windows can use the port at a time.

Upload fails with “port busy”?

Close other programs that use the COM port (another IDE window, PuTTY, a Python script).

docs.title: The breadboard
docs.text:
• Build and test circuits before soldering; debug designs quickly.

  • Side rails (power rails): long strips for VCC (red, +) and GND (blue, \(-\)).

  • Terminal strips: each row of 5 holes is connected.

  • The centre gap separates the two halves: no connection across it. Chips (DIP) straddle it.

  • Use colour-coded jumper wires: red = 3.3 V/5 V, black = GND, other colours = signals.

Long breadboards

On some boards the power rails are split in the middle: bridge them with a wire.

Sources: Figure: lecture 4 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: How the strips are connected
docs.text:
Rule

Two legs in the same strip are connected. Two legs in different strips only connect through a wire or component.

ESP32 DevKit on a breadboard

The DevKit is wide: it covers almost both halves. Use two breadboards side by side, or only one row of free holes.

docs.title: Common breadboard mistakes
docs.text:
1. Both legs of a resistor or LED in the same strip: the component is shorted.

  2. Component placed along the gap instead of across it.

  3. Power rail split in the middle, half the board has no power.

  4. 5 V on a rail that also feeds 3.3 V parts.

  5. LED inserted the wrong way round (long leg = anode = +).

  6. Loose wires: push them in fully, keep them short and flat.

Build step by step

  1. Connect GND and 3.3 V rails, measure them.

  2. Add one component, test with a small sketch.

  3. Add the next one only when the first works.

Document

Take a photo of the working setup and draw the wiring (e.g. Fritzing, draw.io, Wokwi): you need it for the report.

docs.title: Libraries: standing on the shoulders of others
docs.text:
• A library is ready-made code for a task or a device: you call its functions instead of writing everything yourself.

  • Built into the ESP32 core: Wire (I2C), SPI, WiFi, Preferences, Ticker, WebServer …

  • External, via the Library Manager: sensor and display drivers (DHT, BME280, SSD1306, PubSubClient …).

Workflow for every new library

  1. Install: Sketch \(\rightarrow\) Include Library \(\rightarrow\) Manage Libraries, search, install (also its dependencies).

  2. Read the example sketch: File \(\rightarrow\) Examples \(\rightarrow\) \<library>.

  3. Add #include <LibraryName.h>.

  4. Create the required object.

  5. Call its initialisation in setup().

  6. Use its functions in loop() or your own functions.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation

Under the hood: what a library does for you
docs.text:
• display.begin() sends a list of command bytes over I2C, for example Wire.write(0xAE): “display off”, then contrast, addressing mode, … “display on”.

  • Those numbers come from the datasheet of the SSD1306 controller.

  • The library author read the datasheet so you do not have to, but you can, and sometimes must.

Yes, hex

Registers, commands and addresses are written in hexadecimal: 0xAE, 0x3C, 0x76. That is why we practised it.

Choose libraries carefully

Popular, maintained, with examples and compatible with the ESP32 core 3.x. Check the date of the last update.

docs.title: Your own library: why and what?
docs.text:
Why write a library?

  • Reuse the same code in every project, without copy-paste.

  • Hide details (pins, registers, timing) behind clear names.

  • Share with your project team, or publish it on GitHub.

  • Fix a bug once: every project that uses the library benefits.

From functions to libraries

A library is the next step after functions: you group related functions (or a class) in their own files.

What is inside?

#include 'x.h' vs <x.h>

Quotes: file in your sketch folder. Angle brackets: an installed library.

docs.title: Good practices for your own library
docs.text:
• Unique names: a prefix or a class avoids clashes with other libraries (boardBegin, not begin).

  • Configurable: pins via the constructor or begin(pin), not hard-coded where possible.

  • Non-blocking: no long delay() inside; offer an update() for loop().

  • Private by default: static helpers and private: members.

  • Document every function in the header (what, units, ranges).

  • Ship at least one example sketch per feature.

  • Test each function on its own before using the library in a project.

  • Version it and keep it in Git.

Include guards

#pragma once is short and supported everywhere in Arduino. The classic form is #ifndef COURSEBOARD_H / #define COURSEBOARD_H … #endif.

docs.title: Quiz: spot the error
Debugging strategies
docs.text:
General tools

  1. Print statements with labels: Serial.printf("state=%d t=%.1f\ n", \dots).

  2. LED indicators: light an LED when the code reaches a point (no Serial needed).

  3. Comment out parts: divide and conquer until the problem disappears.

  4. Minimal example: copy only the failing part into a new sketch.

  5. Test one thing at a time; change one thing at a time.

Think like a detective

  • What did you expect? What happened?

  • When did it last work? What changed since then?

  • Is it hardware or software? Swap one: other board, other LED, known-good example sketch.

  • Explain the code line by line to someone else (“rubber duck”).

The most important skill

Not writing code that works the first time, but understanding why it does not work and knowing how to investigate it.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Hardware or software? The LED that does not turn off
docs.text:
The symptom

“My LED turns on, but it never turns off, even though my code writes LOW.”

  • Measure the pin with a multimeter: does the voltage change?

  • Print what the code thinks it is doing.

  • Try the LED on another pin with the Blink example.

Possible causes

  1. The LED is wired to 3V3 instead of the GPIO.

  2. Code and wiring use different pin numbers.

  3. The LOW line is never reached (logic error, wrong if).

  4. Another line writes HIGH right after.

  5. pinMode() missing: the pin is an input with pull-up, the LED glows.

  6. LED wired to a pin that is HIGH at boot or used by something else.

Sources: Example from lecture 4 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: The buttons: active HIGH with hardware debounce
docs.text:
Try simulation: Button debouncing

  • Released: the 3.3 k\(\Omega\) resistor pulls the pin to GND \(\Rightarrow\) LOW.

  • Pressed: the switch connects the pin to 3.3 V \(\Rightarrow\) HIGH.

  • The 220 pF capacitor removes only very short spikes (\(\tau = RC \approx 0.7\) μs).

  • External pull-downs on the board: use INPUT. GPIO34/35 are input only, without internal pulls.

In code

pinMode(34, INPUT); bool pressed = \ \ digitalRead(34) == HIGH;

One press can still give several edges: debounce in software.

docs.title: Digital signals: only two values
docs.text:
Try simulation: Digital I/O

  • A digital signal is either HIGH (1, 3.3 V) or LOW (0, 0 V).

  • It tells you yes or no, not how much: a button is pressed or not.

  • Three functions do almost all the work:

  • pinMode(pin, mode): configure the pin

  • digitalWrite(pin, value): set an output

  • digitalRead(pin): read an input

Digital vs analog

Analog: any voltage between 0 and 3.3 V (next chapters). Digital: we only care whether it is low or high.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: pinMode(): configure before use
docs.text:
l L5.2cm L5.4cm **Mode** & **What the pin does** & **Use it for** `OUTPUT` & drives 0 V or 3.3 V & LEDs, transistor bases, relay modules, buzzers `INPUT` & high impedance: only listens & signals that are always driven; buttons **with** an external resistor (course board) `INPUT_PULLUP` & listens + internal $\approx$45 k$\Omega$ resistor to 3.3 V & a button to GND without external resistor (pressed = LOW) `INPUT_PULLDOWN` & listens + internal resistor to GND & a button to 3.3 V without external resistor (pressed = HIGH)

Where?

Call pinMode() once in setup() for every pin you use.

GPIO 34–39

Input only, no internal pull-up or pull-down: INPUT_PULLUP silently does nothing.

Sources: Arduino Language Reference; ESP-IDF Programming Guide: GPIO & RTC GPIO (ESP32)

docs.title: digitalWrite(): switching an output
docs.text:
Try simulation: Digital I/O

led_on.ino
// Version 1: magic numbers
void setup() {
  pinMode(23, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(23, HIGH);
}
void loop() {}

Download this example

led_on_const.ino
// Version 2: a named constant
const int LED_BLUE = 23;

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_BLUE, OUTPUT);     // pin as output
  digitalWrite(LED_BLUE, HIGH);  // 3.3 V: LED on
}
void loop() {}

Download this example

  • HIGH puts 3.3 V on the pin; current flows through resistor and LED to GND.

  • LOW puts 0 V on the pin: no current, LED off.

  • Both versions do the same, but version 2 is readable and changing the pin means one edit.

Rule

No “magic numbers” in your code: give every pin and every setting a const with a meaningful name.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

Example: all four LEDs of the course board
digitalRead(): what counts as HIGH or LOW?
docs.text:
Try simulation: Digital I/O

  • digitalRead(pin) returns HIGH or LOW: yes or no, not how much.

  • Store the result: bool pressed = digitalRead(34);

  • Between the thresholds the result is undefined: it may flip randomly.

  • Lecture rule of thumb: LOW \(\leq\) 0.8 V, HIGH \(\geq\) 2.4 V.

5 V signals

Reduce them to \(\approx\) 3.3 V or less before they reach a GPIO (voltage divider, level shifter).

Sources: ESP32 Series Datasheet; Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Floating inputs and pull resistors
docs.text:
Try simulation: Pull-up / pull-down

Floating

Open button: the pin is connected to nothing. It picks up noise \(\Rightarrow\) random readings.

Pull-down

Resistor to GND: released = LOW, pressed = HIGH. Course board.

Pull-up

Resistor to 3.3 V: released = HIGH, pressed = LOW (“active low”).

Why a resistor and not a wire?

When the button is pressed, the resistor limits the current from 3.3 V to GND to a few μA–mA instead of a short circuit. Typical values: 3.3–47 k\(\Omega\).

docs.title: External pull resistor? Configure the pin as INPUT
docs.text:
The resistor already does the job in hardware

An external pull-up or pull-down already sets the released level. Use pinMode(BUTTON, INPUT); to configure the input; no internal pull needs to be enabled.

@L5.6cml c c@ **Button circuit (normally open)** & **Software mode** & **Released** & **Pressed** External pull-down; button to 3V3 & `INPUT` & LOW & HIGH External pull-up; button to GND & `INPUT` & HIGH & LOW No external resistor; button to GND & `INPUT_PULLUP`\* & HIGH & LOW No external resistor; button to 3V3 & `INPUT_PULLDOWN`\* & LOW & HIGH

* Only on GPIOs that support internal pull resistors.

INPUT does not disconnect an external resistor

It disables internal pulls, leaving the external resistor connected. With no pull resistor, an open button leaves the high-impedance input floating.

Course board: KEY1 and KEY2

GPIO34/35 already have external pull-downs: use INPUT; pressed is HIGH. These classic ESP32 pins have no internal pull resistors.

Sources: Arduino-ESP32 GPIO modes; course-board schematic

docs.title: Reading the course-board buttons
docs.text:
Try simulation: Pull-up / pull-down

buttons.ino
const int KEY1 = 34;        // active HIGH (pull-down)
const int KEY2 = 35;
const int LED_BLUE = 23;
const int LED_RED  = 21;
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(KEY1, INPUT);     // no internal pull on 34/35
  pinMode(KEY2, INPUT);
  pinMode(LED_BLUE, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(LED_RED, OUTPUT);
}
void loop() {
  bool key1 = digitalRead(KEY1);   // true = pressed
  bool key2 = digitalRead(KEY2);
  digitalWrite(LED_BLUE, key1);    // LED follows button
  digitalWrite(LED_RED, key2);
  Serial.printf("KEY1=%d KEY2=%d\n", key1, key2);
  delay(100);
}

Download this example

  • Each LED follows its button: pressed = on.

  • digitalRead() returns HIGH/LOW, which equals true/false: you can store it in a bool.

  • The Serial Monitor shows the raw state: the first test for any input.

Breadboard version

Button to GND on GPIO25, with no external pull-up? Use INPUT_PULLUP; pressed = LOW. If an external pull-up is already fitted, use INPUT instead.

docs.title: Level vs edge: toggling an LED
docs.text:
Try simulation: Button debouncing

toggle.ino
const int KEY1 = 34;
const int LED_GREEN = 22;

bool ledOn = false;
bool lastKey = LOW;

void setup() {
  pinMode(KEY1, INPUT);
  pinMode(LED_GREEN, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  bool key = digitalRead(KEY1);
  if (key == HIGH && lastKey == LOW) {  // rising edge
    ledOn = !ledOn;                     // toggle
    digitalWrite(LED_GREEN, ledOn);
  }
  lastKey = key;                        // remember
  delay(10);
}

Download this example

  • Level: “is the button pressed now?”

  • Edge: “did it become pressed since last time?”

  • Compare the current reading with the previous one, stored in a variable.

  • !ledOn inverts a bool.

Sources: Arduino Language Reference

docs.title: Flowchart: edge detection (toggle)
docs.text:
Try simulation: Digital I/O

Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

  • The decision compares now with last time: only a change from LOW to HIGH (an edge) toggles the LED.

  • lastKey = key is executed on both paths: the program must always remember the latest state.

  • Holding the button does nothing more: the condition is only true once per press.

docs.title: Driving bigger loads: use a transistor
docs.text:
• A GPIO can deliver only \(\approx\) 12–20 mA at 3.3 V.

  • Motors, pumps, relays and LED strips need more current and often 5–12 V.

  • The GPIO switches a transistor (or MOSFET), which switches the load.

  • Inductive loads (motor, relay coil) need a flyback diode across them.

  • Common ground between ESP32 and load supply.

Easy option

Ready-made relay or MOSFET modules contain transistor and diode.

docs.title: Quiz: digital I/O
docs.text:
1. You forgot pinMode(23, OUTPUT). What happens with digitalWrite(23, HIGH)?

    Check your answer

    The pin stays an input; at best the LED glows very faintly. Always configure the mode.

  2. A button on GPIO35 (to GND, no resistor) gives random values. Why?

    Check your answer

    GPIO35 has no internal pull-up and nothing pulls it HIGH: the input floats.

  3. With INPUT_PULLUP, what does a pressed button read?

    Check your answer

    LOW: the button connects the pin to GND.

  4. Your toggle program sometimes switches twice per press. Name the cause.

    Check your answer

    Contact bounce: one press produces several edges (see chapter Time and Interrupts).

  5. Can a GPIO drive a 12 V water pump directly?

    Check your answer

    No: use a transistor/MOSFET or relay module and a separate supply.

docs.title: Why flowcharts?
docs.text:
Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

  • A visual diagram of a program or process.

  • Synchronise understanding with the client: does the drawing match what they want?

  • Design the code before typing it.

  • Find logic errors early: a missing “no” branch is easy to see.

  • Explain and document your program in reports.

In this course

Every assignment contains a flowchart. It is part of the assessment.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: The standard symbols
docs.text:
Good habits

  • Flow from top to bottom, left to right.

  • Label every decision exit (yes / no).

  • One idea per box, in plain words.

  • Loops go back up with a clear arrow.

Common mistakes

  • A decision with only one exit.

  • Arrows that cross or have no direction.

  • Code syntax inside boxes instead of meaning.

  • No way back to the start (program “ends”).

docs.title: Example 1: blink as a flowchart
docs.text:
Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

const int LED_PIN = 23;      // blue LED

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);  // LED pin = output
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);   // LED on
  delay(500);                    // wait 500 ms
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);    // LED off
  delay(500);                    // wait 500 ms
}

Download this example

One box = one or a few lines

The comments in the code use the same words as the boxes: the flowchart and the code tell the same story.

docs.text:

docs.text:
1. Read num1 and num2.

  2. Ask whether num1 > num2.

  3. True: display num1; false: display num2.

Check the boundary

What happens when both numbers are equal? The false branch displays num2, which is also the correct maximum.

  2. A decision diamond has three arrows going out. Is that allowed?

    Check your answer

docs.title: Functions: give a name to a job
docs.text:
Try simulation: Functions

  • A function is a block of code with a name that you can call whenever you need it.

  • You already use many: pinMode(), digitalWrite(), Serial.println(), setup(), loop().

  • It can take parameters (input) and return a value (output), or neither.

  • Benefits: less repetition, readable code, test one piece at a time, reuse in the next project.

name(parameters) { // code }

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Functions without parameters and return value
Parameters: functions with input
docs.text:
Try simulation: Functions

blink_times.ino
void blinkTimes(int pin, int times, int ms) {
  for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) {
    digitalWrite(pin, HIGH);
    delay(ms);
    digitalWrite(pin, LOW);
    delay(ms);
  }
}

void setup() {
  pinMode(23, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(21, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  blinkTimes(23, 3, 200);   // blue: 3 fast blinks
  blinkTimes(21, 1, 1000);  // red: 1 slow blink
}

Download this example

  • Parameters are local variables that receive a copy of the values in the call.

  • The order and type must match: pin, times, ms.

  • One function, many behaviours: that is reuse.

Pass by value

Changing times inside the function does not change the variable of the caller: the function works on a copy.

docs.title: Flowchart: calling a function
docs.text:
Try simulation: Functions

Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

  • The box with double side lines is a function call (“predefined process”).

  • The function has its own flowchart: it starts with its name and ends with return.

  • After return the caller continues with the next box.

  • Two calls with different parameters, one flowchart for the function.

docs.title: Return values: functions with output
docs.text:
Try simulation: Functions

convert.ino
const int POT_PIN = 36;
float convertToVoltage(int adcValue) {
  return adcValue * 3.3 / 4095.0;    // 12-bit ADC
}
bool isAbove(float value, float limit) {
  return value > limit;
}
void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); }
void loop() {
  int raw = analogRead(POT_PIN);
  float voltage = convertToVoltage(raw);
  Serial.printf("raw=%d  V=%.2f\n", raw, voltage);
  if (isAbove(voltage, 2.0)) {
    Serial.println("Above 2 V!");
  }
  delay(500);
}

Download this example

  • The return type before the name says what comes back: float, bool, int …

  • return ends the function immediately and hands back the value.

  • The call can be used like a value: in an assignment, a print, a condition.

From an Uno example?

* 5.0 / 1023.0 is for a 10-bit, 5 V Uno. ESP32: * 3.3 / 4095.0.

docs.title: Example: geometric figures
docs.text:
Try simulation: Functions

geometry.ino
// PI is already defined by Arduino.h
float circleArea(float r)             { return PI * r * r; }
float circleCircumference(float r)    { return 2 * PI * r; }
float rectangleArea(float w, float h) { return w * h; }
float triangleArea(float b, float h)  { return 0.5 * b * h; }

float cylinderVolume(float r, float h) {
  return circleArea(r) * h;           // a function using a function
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  Serial.printf("circle r=2:       %.2f\n", circleArea(2));
  Serial.printf("circumference:    %.2f\n", circleCircumference(2));
  Serial.printf("rectangle 3 x 4:  %.2f\n", rectangleArea(3, 4));
  Serial.printf("triangle 6, 2:    %.2f\n", triangleArea(6, 2));
  Serial.printf("cylinder r=1 h=5: %.2f\n", cylinderVolume(1, 5));
  float total = circleArea(1) + rectangleArea(2, 3);  // in an expression
  Serial.printf("total area:       %.2f\n", total);
}
void loop() {}

Download this example

  • Each function has one job and a name that says it.

  • Different numbers of parameters: 1 (r) or 2 (w, h).

  • A call is a value: use it in a print, an assignment or an expression.

  • Functions can call other functions: cylinderVolume() reuses circleArea().

Test like a mathematician

Check each function with values you can compute by hand: \(r = 1 \Rightarrow \pi\).

if: making decisions
docs.text:
Try simulation: Conditionals

if.ino
// if: do something only when true
if (temperature > 30) {
  digitalWrite(LED_RED, HIGH);
}

// if / else: choose between two
if (temperature > 30) {
  digitalWrite(LED_RED, HIGH);
} else {
  digitalWrite(LED_RED, LOW);
}

// else if: choose between many
if (temperature > 30) {
  Serial.println("hot");
} else if (temperature > 20) {
  Serial.println("warm");
} else {
  Serial.println("cold");
}

Download this example

  • The condition in ( ) is true or false.

  • Only the block of the first true condition runs; the rest is skipped.

  • else catches everything that was not true before.

  • Order matters: test the most specific case first.

Flowchart link

Every if is a decision diamond; else if is a second diamond on the “no” exit.

Sources: Examples from lecture 2 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

Comparison and logical operators
docs.text:
Try simulation: Conditionals

Op. Meaning Example (x = 5) == equal to x == 5 \(\rightarrow\) true != not equal x != 5 \(\rightarrow\) false > < greater / less x > 3 \(\rightarrow\) true >= <= or equal x <= 4 \(\rightarrow\) false ! not !(x > 3) \(\rightarrow\) false && and x > 0 && x < 10 \(\rightarrow\) true || or x < 0 || x > 10 \(\rightarrow\) false A B A && B A || B F F F F F T F T T F F T T T T T

= is not ==

if (x = 0) assigns 0 to x and is always false. The compiler only warns. Write if (x == 0).

docs.title: Combining conditions
docs.text:
Try simulation: Conditionals

conditions.ino
// inside a range: AND
if (temperature > 20 && temperature < 30) {
  Serial.println("comfortable");
}

// outside a range: OR
if (temperature < 10 || temperature > 30) {
  digitalWrite(LED_RED, HIGH);      // alarm
}

// buttons: both, either, exactly one
bool k1 = digitalRead(34);
bool k2 = digitalRead(35);
if (k1 && k2)  Serial.println("both");
if (k1 || k2)  Serial.println("at least one");
if (k1 != k2)  Serial.println("exactly one");
if (!k1)       Serial.println("KEY1 released");

Download this example

  • &&: all parts must be true.

  • ||: at least one part true.

  • != between two bools is an exclusive or.

  • Use brackets when mixing: (a && b) || c.

A classic bug

if (t > 20 || t < 30) is always true: every number is above 20 or below 30.

docs.title: Flowchart: combining conditions with && and ||
docs.text:
Try simulation: Conditionals

  • AND (&&): two decisions in a row; every no skips the action.

  • OR (||): two ways to reach the action; one yes is enough.

  • The second question is skipped when the first already decides (“short-circuit evaluation”).

docs.title: Example: a thermostat with hysteresis
docs.text:
Try simulation: Hysteresis

Try simulation: Heating and cooling

thermostat.ino
const int POT_PIN = 36;     // pot simulates 0..30 C
const int HEATER  = 21;     // red LED = heater
const float T_ON  = 19.0;   // switch on below
const float T_OFF = 21.0;   // switch off above
bool heaterOn = false;
float readTemperature() {
  return analogRead(POT_PIN) * 30.0 / 4095.0;
}
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(HEATER, OUTPUT);
}
void loop() {
  float t = readTemperature();
  if (!heaterOn && t < T_ON) {
    heaterOn = true;
  } else if (heaterOn && t > T_OFF) {
    heaterOn = false;
  }
  digitalWrite(HEATER, heaterOn);
  Serial.printf("T=%.1f heater=%d\n", t, heaterOn);
  delay(500);
}

Download this example

  • One threshold would switch on/off many times per second around 20 °C (“chattering”).

  • Two thresholds = hysteresis: stable switching.

  • The decision depends on the state (heaterOn): a first taste of state machines.

docs.title: Flowchart: thermostat with hysteresis
docs.text:
Try simulation: Hysteresis

Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

  • The decisions use the input and the current state (heaterOn).

  • Between 19 and 21 °C both answers are no: nothing changes, so the heater does not chatter.

  • This is the same logic as the code on the previous section, box for box.

docs.text:
1. What is printed? int x = 7; if (x > 5) { x = 2; } else if (x > 1) { x = 3; } then Serial.println(x);

    Check your answer

  2. Write the condition “temperature between 18 and 24, inclusive”.

    Check your answer

    t >= 18 && t <= 24

  3. What does a function with return type void return?

    Check your answer

    Nothing. It is called for its effect (e.g. switching LEDs).

  4. float half(int x) { return x / 2; } returns 3.0 for half(7). Fix it.

    Check your answer

    return x / 2.0; (integer division otherwise).

  5. Why does a thermostat need two thresholds?

    Check your answer

    Hysteresis prevents rapid on/off switching when the temperature is near the setpoint.

docs.title: A short history of programming
docs.text:
The trend

Each generation hides details of the machine so humans can think about the problem instead of the hardware.

Where are we?

Arduino sketches are written in C++ (1985), built on C (1972). Still the language of embedded systems.

Sources: The C Programming Language; Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Programming languages: the original lecture overview
docs.text:
• The original overview places assembly, FORTRAN, COBOL, BASIC, C, C++, Python, Java and other languages on a common timeline.

  • Different languages suit different problems; they do not simply replace their predecessors.

  • This course uses Arduino C++ to connect programming concepts to hardware.

  • The marked C++ and Python entries invite a comparison of compiled firmware and interpreted programs.

Discussion

Which names do you recognise? Which have you used, and for what purpose?

Sources: Original figure, lecture 1 slide 14 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: From client story to program
docs.text:
Version 1: what clients often say

“I want my plant pots to take care of themselves. Make it happen.”

Version 2: a useful story

“When the plant needs water, the pot should water it. I also want the pot to tell me what is going on, because I don’t always know if the soil is wet or dry. The system should check how wet the soil is, decide whether to water, and tell me what it did.”

Turn it into measurable requirements

  1. Needs water = soil humidity \(<\) 30 %.

  2. Give water = pump on for 10 s.

  3. Report humidity and action over Serial.

  4. Check again every minute.

Ask the client

What is “dry”? How much water? How often? What if the tank is empty? Vague words become numbers.

Sources: Example from lecture 1 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.text:
• Almost every embedded system follows this pattern: read \(\rightarrow\) decide \(\rightarrow\) act, forever.

  • In Arduino this “forever” is the loop() function.

  • Before coding: list every input and output with its type (digital, analog, bus) and pin.

docs.title: From source code to a running program
docs.text:
Running process

The executable is loaded and started: it gets memory, CPU time and access to inputs and outputs. On the ESP32 the program starts again at every power-up or reset.

Compiled vs interpreted

Compiled (C/C++): translated once, runs fast, errors found before running. Interpreted (Python): translated while running, easier to try, slower.

docs.title: Three kinds of errors
docs.text:
Syntax error

The code breaks the grammar of the language. The compiler refuses it.

example.cpp
Serial.println("Hi")  // missing ;

Download this example

at compile time: easiest to fix.

Runtime error

Valid code that fails while running: crash, reboot, garbage.

example.cpp
int a = 10;
int b = 0;
int c = a / b;   // divide by 0

Download this example

when it happens: watch the Serial Monitor.

Logic error

The program runs fine but does the wrong thing.

example.cpp
int sum = 10 + 20 + 30;
int avg = sum / 4;  // 3 values!

Download this example

only by testing against the requirements: hardest.

Info

The compiler only catches the first kind. That is why every assignment has a test / evaluation part.

Sources: Examples from lecture 1 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Quiz: what kind of error?
docs.text:
1. digitalwrite(2, HIGH); does not compile.

    Check your answer

    Syntax error: C++ is case sensitive, the function is digitalWrite.

  2. The LED blinks twice per second, the requirement says once per second.

    Check your answer

    Logic error: the program runs, but the delay values are wrong.

  3. The board reboots every time you read element 1000 of a 10-element array.

    Check your answer

    Runtime error: reading outside the array touches memory that is not yours.

  4. int x = 10 followed by void setup() gives expected ’,’ or ’;’ before ’void’.

    Check your answer

    Syntax error: the missing ; is on the line before the one the compiler points at.

  5. The pump keeps running when the soil is already wet.

    Check your answer

    Logic error, e.g. the comparison is > instead of <.

docs.title: I2C at a glance
docs.text:
Try simulation: I2C

  • I2C: Inter-Integrated Circuit (Philips, 1982).

  • Serial communication with multiple devices on the same wires.

  • Only two signal wires (+ VCC and GND):

  • SDA: data

  • SCL: clock (timing)

  • One master (controller), several slaves (targets), each with an address.

  • Typical speeds: 100 kHz (standard), 400 kHz (fast).

Sources: Figure: panoxdisplay.com, via lecture 5 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; UM10204: I2C-bus specification and user manual, Rev. 7.0

docs.title: Master and slaves
docs.text:
Master (e.g. the ESP32)

  • controls the communication;

  • generates the clock signal on SCL;

  • starts every transfer;

  • requests data from a slave.

Slave (sensor, display, memory)

  • only responds to master requests;

  • every I2C device has an address (7 bits);

  • other devices ignore requests not meant for them.

Example: the BME280 answers to 0x76. The ESP32 sends “0x76, give me register 0xF7”: only the BME280 reacts.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Pull-up resistors and open-drain lines
docs.text:
• The pull-up resistors make the lines HIGH by default.

  • Devices can only pull the line LOW (“open drain”); they never drive it HIGH.

  • So two devices can never short-circuit each other, even if both talk at once.

  • Pull-ups are often already on the sensor board.

  • The internal ESP32 pull-ups (\(\approx\) 45 k\(\Omega\)) are too weak for reliable I2C: use 2.2–10 k\(\Omega\).

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; UM10204: I2C-bus specification and user manual, Rev. 7.0

docs.title: A transaction, step by step (1/2)
docs.text:
Try simulation: I2C

1. Start condition

The master pulls SDA LOW while SCL is HIGH. All slaves start listening.

2. Address + read/write

The master sends the 7-bit address and 1 bit: R/W (0 = write, 1 = read). The addressed slave answers with ACK (pulls SDA LOW).

Rule

Data on SDA may only change while SCL is LOW. A change while SCL is HIGH is a START or STOP condition.

Sources: Figures: Rheingold Heavy I2C Signals, via lecture 5

docs.title: A transaction, step by step (2/2)
docs.text:
Try simulation: I2C

3. Data bytes

8 bits per byte, most significant bit first; the receiver acknowledges every byte.

4. Stop condition

After the last byte the master releases SDA HIGH while SCL is HIGH: the bus is free. Or it sends a repeated start to continue.

Sources: Figures: Rheingold Heavy I2C Signals, via lecture 5

docs.title: Worked example: the bytes on the wire
docs.text:
Try simulation: I2C

Read the chip ID of a BME280 at 0x76

  1. START

  2. Address byte, write: \((0x76 \ll 1) \,|\, 0\) = 0xEC \(\rightarrow\) ACK

  3. Register number 0xD0 (chip ID) \(\rightarrow\) ACK

  4. Repeated START

  5. Address byte, read: \((0x76 \ll 1) \,|\, 1\) = 0xED \(\rightarrow\) ACK

  6. Slave sends 0x60 (BME280) \(\rightarrow\) master NACK

  7. STOP

Why 0xEC?

The 7-bit address 0x76 = 111 0110 is shifted one place left to make room for the R/W bit: 1110 1100 = 0xEC.

BME280 or BMP280?

Chip ID 0x60 = BME280 (with humidity), 0x58 = BMP280 (no humidity). The modules look identical!

Datasheets

Some datasheets give the 8-bit form (0xEC/0xED), libraries use the 7-bit form (0x76).

Sources: BME280 Combined humidity and pressure sensor, datasheet; UM10204: I2C-bus specification and user manual, Rev. 7.0

docs.title: Quiz: I2C
docs.text:
1. Which two signal lines does I2C use, and what does each carry?

    Check your answer

    SDA (data) and SCL (clock).

  2. How does a slave know a message is meant for it?

    Check your answer

    The master sends the 7-bit address first; only the device with that address answers (ACK).

  3. Why do I2C lines need pull-up resistors?

    Check your answer

    Devices can only pull the lines LOW; the resistors provide the HIGH level.

  4. What byte appears on the wire when the master wants to read from address 0x3C?

    Check your answer

    \((0x3C \ll 1) | 1\) = 0x79.

  5. How many addresses does a 7-bit address field allow?

    Check your answer

    128 (some are reserved: about 112 usable).

docs.title: The for loop: repeat a known number of times
docs.text:
Try simulation: Loops

(int i = 0; i \< 10; i++) { … }

for.ino
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  Serial.println(i);      // 0 1 2 ... 9
}

Download this example

  1. int i = 0: create the counter.

  2. i < 10? If false: leave the loop.

  3. Run the body.

  4. i++: add 1, back to step 2.

Counting

Start at 0 and use <: the body runs exactly 10 times (0 … 9). This matches array indices.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Flowchart: the for loop
docs.text:
Try simulation: Loops

Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

(int i = 0; i \< 10; i++) { Serial.println(i); }

  1. init runs once.

  2. condition is checked before every round.

  3. The body runs, then the step; back to 2.

  4. Condition false \(\Rightarrow\) continue after the loop.

Zero rounds

If the condition is false at the start, the body never runs.

docs.title: for loops in practice
docs.text:
Try simulation: Loops

for_examples.ino
// blink 5 times
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  digitalWrite(23, HIGH); delay(100);
  digitalWrite(23, LOW);  delay(100);
}

// count down 10, 9, ... 1
for (int i = 10; i > 0; i--) {
  Serial.println(i);
}

// even numbers 0, 2, ... 20
for (int i = 0; i <= 20; i += 2) {
  Serial.println(i);
}

Download this example

nested.ino
// nested loops: multiplication table
for (int row = 1; row <= 5; row++) {
  for (int col = 1; col <= 5; col++) {
    Serial.printf("%4d", row * col);
  }
  Serial.println();
}

Download this example

  • The step can be anything: i--, i += 2, i *= 2.

  • Nested loops: the inner loop runs completely for every round of the outer loop (5 \(\times\) 5 = 25 prints).

  • %4d prints a number in a 4-character column.

docs.title: The while loop: repeat until something happens
docs.text:
Try simulation: Loops

while.ino
// keep reading until the pot is high
int value = analogRead(36);
while (value < 3000) {
  value = analogRead(36);
  delay(10);
}
Serial.println("Threshold reached");

// wait until KEY1 is pressed
while (digitalRead(34) == LOW) {
  // do nothing: just wait
}

// do-while: body runs at least once
int tries = 0;
do {
  tries++;
} while (tries < 3);

Download this example

  • for: you know how many times.

  • while: you repeat until a condition changes.

  • The condition must be able to change inside the loop, otherwise it never ends.

  • break leaves a loop early; continue skips to the next round.

Loops can block your program

While the ESP32 waits in a while, nothing else happens: no other button, no LED, no Wi-Fi. Prefer if + millis() (chapter Time and Interrupts).

Sources: Examples from lecture 2 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Arrays: many values under one name
Arrays + loops: a perfect team
docs.text:
Try simulation: Loops

samples.ino
const int N = 10;
int samples[N];

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);

  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {     // fill
    samples[i] = analogRead(36);
    delay(20);
  }

  long sum = 0;                     // average
  int minV = samples[0];
  int maxV = samples[0];
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    sum += samples[i];
    if (samples[i] < minV) minV = samples[i];
    if (samples[i] > maxV) maxV = samples[i];
  }
  Serial.printf("avg=%ld min=%d max=%d\n",
                sum / N, minV, maxV);
}

void loop() {}

Download this example

  • The loop counter i is used as the index.

  • One loop to fill, one loop to process.

  • sum is a long: 10 \(\times\) 4095 fits in an int on the ESP32, but not on an Uno.

  • Min/max: start with the first element, then compare every other one.

Why average?

ADC readings are noisy. The average of 10 samples is much more stable than one sample.

Sources: Adapted from lecture 2 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: What is a GPIO?
docs.text:
• General Purpose Input/Output: a pin your program controls.

  • As output: the pin is 0 V (LOW) or 3.3 V (HIGH).

  • As input: the program reads whether the voltage is low or high.

  • Most pins have extra functions: ADC, touch, PWM, UART, I2C, SPI …

  • In code you use the GPIO number, not the physical pin position.

Labels on the board

“D23” on the DevKit silkscreen means GPIO23 \(\Rightarrow\) in code: 23.

docs.title: How to read a pinout diagram
docs.text:
1. Find the orientation: USB connector, antenna, buttons.

  2. Each pin shows its name (D23, VP, TX0) and functions (ADC, DAC, touch).

  3. Power pins (3V3, VIN, GND) cannot be used as I/O.

  4. Read the notes: forbidden pins, Wi-Fi conflicts.

  5. Different boards have different pinouts: always use the one of your board.

docs.title: Forbidden pins and boot-sensitive pins
docs.text:
GPIO 6–11 Forbidden

Connected to the internal SPI flash (SD0–SD3, CMD, CLK). Using them crashes the chip. Exposed only on 38-pin boards.

GPIO 0, 2, 5, 12, 15 Strapping pins

Sampled at reset to choose boot mode / flash voltage. External pull-ups / pull-downs can make the board fail to boot or to upload.

GPIO 34, 35, 36, 39 Input only

No output driver and no internal pull-up / pull-down. Use external resistors.

Sources: ESP32 Series Datasheet; ESP-IDF Programming Guide: GPIO & RTC GPIO (ESP32); ESP32 Pinout Reference: Which GPIO pins should you use?

docs.title: Risky pins: think twice
docs.text:
GPIO 1, 3 UART0

TX0 / RX0 are wired to the USB bridge: used for upload and Serial. Debug text appears on TX at boot.

ADC2 Wi-Fi conflict

ADC2 (GPIO 0, 2, 4, 12–15, 25–27) cannot be read while Wi-Fi is on. Use ADC1 (GPIO 32–39).

GPIO 14 and GPIO 5, 15

Output a short PWM / HIGH pulse at boot: avoid them for relays or motors.

5 V Never on a GPIO

I/O pins are 3.3 V only. Use a level shifter or a divider.

Sources: ESP32 Series Datasheet; ESP-IDF Programming Guide: GPIO & RTC GPIO (ESP32); ESP32 Pinout Reference: Which GPIO pins should you use?

c c L4.6cm L4.8cm **Pin** & **Default** & **Function at reset** & **Rule of thumb** `GPIO0` & pull-up & HIGH = run from flash, LOW = **download mode** & Do not hold LOW at reset (BOOT button does this on purpose) `GPIO2` & pull-down & Must be LOW / floating to enter download mode & Avoid pull-ups; LED is fine `GPIO12` & pull-down & Selects flash voltage: HIGH = **1.8 V** & Never HIGH at boot with 3.3 V flash $\rightarrow$ boot loop `GPIO15` & pull-up & LOW silences the boot log on UART0 & Keep HIGH or floating `GPIO5` & pull-up & SDIO slave timing & Keep HIGH or floating

Typical symptom

“Failed to connect to ESP32: Timed out waiting for packet header” or a reboot loop \(\rightarrow\) check what is connected to the strapping pins.

docs.title: Electrical limits and pin cheat sheet
docs.text:
Electrical rules

  • Logic level 3.3 V; \(V_{IH} \geq 0.75\,V_{DD}\), \(V_{IL} \leq 0.25\,V_{DD}\).

  • Source up to \(\approx\) 40 mA per pin (absolute), keep loads \(\leq\) 12–20 mA: use transistors / drivers for relays, motors, LED strips.

  • Internal pull-up / pull-down \(\approx\) 45 k\(\Omega\).

  • ADC: 0–3.1 V with 11 dB attenuation, non-linear near the ends; use analogReadMilliVolts().

  • VIN accepts 5 V; 3V3 pin supplies small sensors only.

Which pin for what?

@L1.9cm L4.5cm@ Digital out & `4` `13` `16` `17` `18` `19` `21` & `22` `23` `25` `26` `27` `32` `33` Analog in & `32--39` (ADC1, works with Wi-Fi) Analog out & `25` `26` (DAC) I2C & SDA `21` SCL `22` SPI (VSPI) & `23` `19` `18` `5` UART2 & RX `16` TX `17` Touch & `4` `13` `27` `32` `33`

Sources: ESP32 Series Datasheet; ESP32 Pinout Reference: Which GPIO pins should you use?

docs.title: Worked example: the series resistor of an LED
docs.text:
1. Ohm’s law over the resistor: \(R = \dfrac{V_{pin} - V_F}{I}\)

  2. Blue LED: \(V_F \approx 3.0\) V; wanted current \(I = 5\) mA.

  3. \(R = (3.3 - 3.0) / 0.005 = 60\,\Omega\) \(\rightarrow\) the board uses 47 \(\Omega\) (6.4 mA).

  4. Red LED: \(V_F \approx 2.0\) V \(\Rightarrow\) \(R = 1.3/0.005 = 260\,\Omega\) \(\rightarrow\) 255 \(\Omega\) on the board.

Never without a resistor

Without \(R\) the current is limited only by the pin: the LED and the GPIO can be damaged.

docs.title: Quiz: choose the right pin
docs.text:
1. You need an extra output for a relay module. Is GPIO12 a good choice?

    Check your answer

    No: GPIO12 is a strapping pin; a pull-up on it at boot selects 1.8 V flash. Take e.g. GPIO25 or 26.

  2. A potentiometer must be read while Wi-Fi is active. Which pins are allowed?

    Check your answer

    ADC1 pins: GPIO 32--39 (on the course board: the AD1/AD2 terminals, GPIO36/39).

  3. Can you write digitalWrite(35, HIGH)?

    Check your answer

    No effect: GPIO 34--39 are input only.

  4. The board does not boot when your circuit is attached, but works when it is removed. First suspect?

    Check your answer

    Something connected to a strapping pin (0, 2, 5, 12, 15).

  5. Why should GPIO 6–11 never appear in your code?

    Check your answer

    They are connected to the internal SPI flash that holds your program.

docs.title: Advice for the future
docs.text:
• You have learned the fundamentals of embedded programming.

  • You do not need to know every function, library or register by heart: understand the underlying concepts.

  • Break a complex problem into smaller parts.

  • Start small, build something that works, then improve it.

  • Write code that you can explain.

  • Test one thing at a time.

The most important skill

Not writing code that works the first time, but understanding why something does not work and knowing how to investigate it.

Do it yourself!

Some students are more experienced. At some point you will be alone and have to figure it out on your own: practise that now. Build projects that interest you.

Versioning

final, finalv2, reallyreadyfordemo: use Git, especially when you code together.

docs.title: Why serial communication?
docs.text:
Try simulation: UART

A microcontroller talks to a computer to

  • debug: “where is my program now?”

  • display sensor values;

  • check the program state;

  • receive commands;

  • communicate with another device: GPS, another microcontroller, a modem.

Serial vs UART

  • Serial is the concept: bits are sent one after the other over one wire.

  • UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) is the hardware and protocol that does it.

  • I2C and SPI are also serial, but we call them by their own names.

Asynchronous

There is no clock wire: both sides must agree on the speed in advance (the baud rate).

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; UART

docs.title: The UART frame: one byte on the wire
docs.text:
Try simulation: UART

  • Line idles HIGH. A start bit (LOW) wakes up the receiver.

  • 8 data bits, least significant bit first: here 'A' = 65 = 0x41 = 0100 0001.

  • A stop bit (HIGH) ends the frame. “8N1” = 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.

Baud rate math

115 200 baud \(\Rightarrow\) 1 bit \(\approx\) 8.7 μs. 1 byte = 10 bits \(\Rightarrow\) \(\approx\) 11 500 bytes/s. 9600 baud \(\Rightarrow\) only 960 bytes/s.

Sources: UART

docs.title: RX, TX and the UARTs of the ESP32
docs.text:
Try simulation: UART

  • TX (transmit) of one side goes to RX (receive) of the other: crossed.

  • A common GND is required: voltages are measured against it.

  • Both sides must use the same voltage level (3.3 V on the ESP32).

@l l L2.6cm@ **UART** & **RX / TX here** & **Arduino name / use** UART0 & 3 / 1 & `Serial`: USB bridge, upload, Serial Monitor UART1 & 32 / 33 & `Serial1`: pins selected explicitly UART2 & 16 / 17 & `Serial2`: course-board UART terminal

GPIO matrix

Any UART can be routed to other pins: Serial1.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, 25, 26);

Sources: Figure: lecture 2 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: How many UARTs do we have, and which ones?
docs.text:
The classic ESP32 has three independent hardware UART controllers.

@L1.5cm L2.0cm L3.0cm L5.0cm@ **Controller** & **Arduino object** & **RX / TX used here** & **Use on the course board** UART0 & `Serial` & GPIO3 / GPIO1 & USB–UART bridge: upload and Serial Monitor UART1 & `Serial1` & GPIO32 / GPIO33 & Additional device; example pins selected explicitly UART2 & `Serial2` & GPIO16 / GPIO17 & RX2 / TX2 screw terminal on the carrier board

Three controllers, usually two additional links

Keep UART0 for USB debugging; UART1 and UART2 can serve two other devices. HardwareSerial sensor(2) names UART2, not a fourth UART. Counts and available pins differ between ESP32-family chips and modules.

Sources: Classic ESP32 UART count and Arduino objects ESP32 Series Datasheet; Arduino ESP32: Serial (UART)

docs.title: UART number and pin number are different choices
docs.text:
Three serial paths on one board

  • The GPIO matrix routes UART signals to selected suitable pins.

  • In begin(baud, format, RX, TX), the last two numbers choose those pins.

  • The USB socket on this DevKit reaches UART0 through a bridge; it is not a fourth UART.

  • Cross TX to RX and connect a common ground; use compatible 3.3 V logic.

Avoid assumptions from old tutorials

GPIO9/10 are connected to flash on WROOM-32. Do not reuse them for UART1. Choose pins explicitly instead of relying on an example’s defaults.

Sources: UART routing and module pin restrictions ESP32-WROOM-32 Datasheet, Version 3.8; Arduino ESP32: Serial (UART); Espressif: GPIO Matrix and Pin Mux

docs.text:
l L8.6cm **Function** & **What it does** `Serial.begin(115200)` & start the UART at a baud rate (in `setup()`) `Serial.print(x)` / `println(x)` & send text or a number; `println` adds `\ r\ n` `Serial.print(x, HEX)` & print a number in HEX, BIN or DEC `Serial.printf("T=%.1f\ n", t)` & formatted print (ESP32 only): `%d` int, `%f` float, `%s` text `Serial.available()` & number of received bytes waiting in the buffer `Serial.read()` & take one byte from the buffer ($-$1 if empty) `Serial.readStringUntil('\ n')` & read text up to the end of a line (with timeout) `Serial.parseInt()` & read a number from the text `Serial.write(b)` & send a raw byte

docs.title: r and n: a lesson from the typewriter
docs.text:
Try simulation: ASCII characters

Finishing a line took two movements

  1. Carriage return: push the carriage back to the left margin. \(\Rightarrow\) '\ r', CR, ASCII 13

  2. Line feed: turn the roller one line up, so you do not type over the old line. \(\Rightarrow\) '\ n', LF, ASCII 10

  3. Teleprinters (the first serial terminals) copied the typewriter: two separate control characters.

  4. They still travel over every UART today.

So Serial.println('Hi') sends 4 bytes

'H' 72 'i' 105 '\ r' 13 '\ n' 10

Sources: Photo: Dr. Luke, Imperial typewriter, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

What does SERIAL_8N1 mean?
docs.text:
Try simulation: UART

Serial2.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, 16, 17);

  • The frame format: how each byte is packed on the wire, besides the baud rate.

  • Serial.begin(115200) uses SERIAL_8N1 by default.

  • Both devices must use the same format, exactly like the baud rate; otherwise you get garbage or framing errors.

@l c L3.0cm@ **Format** & **bits/byte** & **Typical use** `SERIAL_8N1` & 10 & almost everything: PC, GPS, modules `SERIAL_8E1` & 11 & industrial (Modbus RTU) `SERIAL_7E1` & 10 & old terminals, some meters `SERIAL_8N2` & 11 & slow or picky receivers

Bits per byte

start (1) + data (8) + parity (0) + stop (1) = 10 bits. 9600 baud with 8N1 \(\Rightarrow\) 960 bytes/s; with 8E1 only 872 bytes/s.

Sources: UART; Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation

docs.title: Parity: a simple error check
docs.text:
Try simulation: UART

  • Even parity: the sender adds 1 bit so that the total number of 1s (data + parity) is even.

  • Odd parity: the total number of 1s is odd.

  • The receiver counts again: a mismatch means a bit was flipped by noise.

  • Detects one wrong bit, cannot correct it; two flipped bits go unnoticed.

Char Data bits 1s E bit 'A' 0x41 0100 0001 2 0 'C' 0x43 0100 0011 3 1 'U' 0x55 0101 0101 4 0

In practice

Short cables on a board: SERIAL_8N1. Long, noisy industrial lines: parity (8E1) plus checksums in the message.

docs.title: UART: talking to another device
HardwareSerial: give your UART a name
USB–TTL adapters
docs.text:
• Converts USB from a computer to UART signals at logic level (“TTL” is a historic name).

  • The DevKit has one built in (CP2102/CH340): that is how Serial reaches your laptop.

  • An extra adapter on UART2 gives you a second serial port on the laptop, e.g. to log data while the Serial Monitor shows debug text.

Set the adapter to 3.3 V

Many adapters have a 5 V/3.3 V jumper. 5 V on the ESP32 RX pin can damage it.

Sources: Figures: lectures 2 and 5 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Example: two ESP32 boards talking
Quiz: UART
docs.text:
1. The Serial Monitor shows strange characters. What do you check first?

    Check your answer

    The baud rate in the monitor vs. Serial.begin().

  2. Two boards are connected TX–TX and RX–RX. What happens?

    Check your answer

    Nothing arrives: both transmit on the same wire. Cross the lines: TX \(\rightarrow\) RX.

  3. Why must both boards share GND?

    Check your answer

    A voltage is a difference: without a common reference the receiver cannot tell HIGH from LOW.

  4. How long does it take to send 100 bytes at 9600 baud?

    Check your answer

    \(100 \times 10\) bits \(/ 9600 \approx 0.10\) s.

  5. Why can you not use GPIO 1 and 3 for your own sensor?

    Check your answer

    They are UART0: upload and Serial Monitor go through them.

docs.title: SPI at a glance
docs.text:
• Serial Peripheral Interface: fast serial bus with a clock.

  • Full duplex: data goes in both directions at the same time (I2C is half duplex).

  • No addresses: each slave has its own chip-select (CS / SS) line.

  • Speeds of 10–80 MHz: displays, SD cards, flash memory, fast ADCs.

Sources: Figures: lecture 6 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Basics of the SPI Communication Protocol

docs.title: How an SPI transfer works
docs.text:
1. Master pulls CS LOW: “you, listen”.

  2. Master generates 8 clock pulses on SCK.

  3. With every pulse one bit goes out on MOSI (master out, slave in) and one bit comes in on MISO.

  4. After the last byte: CS HIGH.

Exchange

SPI always exchanges bytes: SPI.transfer(x) sends x and returns the received byte.

docs.title: SPI modes and settings
docs.text:
@l c c L2.6cm@ **Mode** & **CPOL** & **CPHA** & **Clock idle / sample** `SPI_MODE0` & 0 & 0 & idle LOW, rising edge `SPI_MODE1` & 0 & 1 & idle LOW, falling edge `SPI_MODE2` & 1 & 0 & idle HIGH, falling edge `SPI_MODE3` & 1 & 1 & idle HIGH, rising edge

SPISettings(speed, order, mode)

  • Speed: maximum clock the slave accepts (datasheet), e.g. 1 MHz to start.

  • Bit order: MSBFIRST for almost every device.

  • Mode: most devices use mode 0; check the datasheet.

Wrong mode

Data shifted by one bit, or all 0xFF/0x00: first suspect the mode and the CS wiring.

docs.title: SPI: fast, full-duplex
Original SPI diagrams: individual selects and daisy chain
docs.text:
Individual chip-selects

  • SCK, MOSI and MISO are shared.

  • Each device has a separate select wire.

  • Only the selected device drives MISO.

Daisy chain: a different arrangement

  • Devices pass serial data to the next device.

  • The chain shares clock and select.

  • Requires devices that support chaining; check the datasheet.

Sources: Both original diagrams: lecture 6 slide 14 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Basics of the SPI Communication Protocol

docs.text:
UART I2C SPI Signal wires 2 (TX, RX) 2 (SDA, SCL) 3 + 1 CS per slave Clock no (agreed baud) yes yes Devices 2 (point to point) many (addresses) many (chip selects) Duplex full half full Typical speed 9.6–921 kbit/s 100–400 kHz 1–80 MHz Distance metres (RS-232/485) short, on a board short, on a board Typical use PC, GPS, modules sensors, small displays displays, SD card, flash

Which one?

Usually the device decides: read the datasheet. Many sensors support both I2C and SPI (e.g. the BME280).

docs.title: The logic analyzer: seeing your signals
docs.text:
• Records digital signals (HIGH/LOW) on several channels at the same time.

  • Hardware debugging vs software debugging: you see what really happens on the wires.

  • Debug communication (UART, I2C, SPI are decoded into bytes) and timing problems.

  • Cheap 8-channel, 24 MHz analyzers + free PulseView software (sigrok).

Installation (Windows)

Install PulseView; if needed, assign WinUSB to the analyzer using Zadig. Select fx2lafw in PulseView. Older builds may also need the Visual C++ 2010 runtime (x86/x64).

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; PulseView: a Qt based logic analyzer, oscilloscope and MSO GUI for sigrok

docs.title: Capturing a transaction, step by step
docs.text:
1. Connect GND of the analyzer to GND of the circuit (always first!).

  2. Connect channels to the signals: CH0 = SCL, CH1 = SDA (or CS, SCK, MOSI, MISO).

  3. Choose the sample rate: start around 10\(\times\) the bus clock/bit rate or more; also set the sample count for the required time window.

  4. Set a supported trigger: e.g. falling CS (SPI). Falling SDA is a candidate for I2C START; verify that SCL is HIGH.

  5. Capture, then add a protocol decoder.

Signal Sample rate I2C 100 kHz \(\geq\) 1 MHz I2C 400 kHz \(\geq\) 4 MHz UART 115 200 baud 2 MHz to start SPI 1 MHz 12 MHz to start PWM 5 kHz \(\geq\) 500 kHz

Why a trigger?

A trigger selects an event to align the capture with. Available conditions and pre-trigger history depend on the device/driver. Start with no trigger if unsure.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; PulseView: a Qt based logic analyzer, oscilloscope and MSO GUI for sigrok

docs.title: Inside a logic analyzer: voltage becomes sampled bits
docs.text:
1. A probe observes a signal relative to GND.

  2. The input threshold classifies it as 0 or 1.

  3. A sampling clock records all enabled channels at regular intervals.

  4. Software draws the samples. A decoder interprets their pattern as bytes or bus events.

Two different clocks

The ESP32 produces the signal. The analyzer’s independent sample clock observes it: \(\Delta t=1/f_s\). At \(f_s=1\,\mathrm{MHz}\), samples are \(1\,\text{\textmu s}\) apart.

What the trace can tell you

Measure levels, order and timing. Use an oscilloscope to inspect voltage shape, noise and rise time.

docs.title: PulseView: connect the instrument and name the inputs
docs.text:
1. Connect the analyzer by USB; power the ESP32 normally.

  2. Select the real device instead of Demo device. For the common FX2 analyzer: Connect to Device \(\rightarrow\) fx2lafw \(\rightarrow\) USB \(\rightarrow\) Scan \(\rightarrow\) select the device.

  3. Connect analyzer GND to board GND, then the signal probes.

  4. Enable the required inputs. Rename D0/D1 to the signal names to make their role visible.

Input names are not GPIO numbers

D0 means analyzer channel 0. It may be clipped to GPIO23, GPIO17 or any chosen signal.

Windows: assign WinUSB to the analyzer in Zadig if needed; keep the ESP32 USB–UART driver. Select fx2lafw in PulseView. Check input limits for 3.3 V logic; probes observe signals and do not power the circuit.

Sources: PulseView manual: device selection and Windows installation

docs.title: Choose both sample rate and recording length
docs.text:
\(\Delta t=\dfrac{1}{f_s}\qquad T_{\rm capture}=\dfrac{N_s}{f_s}\qquad N_s=f_s\,T_{\rm capture}\)

\(f_s\): samples per second\(N_s\): sample instants per channel\(T_{\rm capture}\): recorded time

@L3.2cmL2.5cmL2.9cmL3.8cm@ **Example signal** & **Sample rate** & **Sample count** & **Resulting window** Blink: 1 Hz & 10 kHz & 50 k samples & 5 s: several full cycles UART: 115200 baud & 2 MHz & 200 k samples & 100 ms: many byte frames I2C: 100 kHz & 2 MHz & 200 k samples & 100 ms: one short transaction I2C: 400 kHz & 8 MHz & 800 k samples & 100 ms: same time, more data

Resolve the shortest feature

Start around 10 samples per bit/clock period or more for decoding; increase for short pulses and timing detail. At 115200 baud, 2 MHz gives about 17 samples per bit.

Faster is not a longer recording

With 100 k samples: 1 MHz records 100 ms; 10 MHz records only 10 ms. Choose the closest supported values and recalculate the window.

docs.title: Blink capture: wire it, set it, run it
Read Blink: period, frequency and duty cycle
docs.text:
• Enable cursors; place them on two consecutive rising edges to measure \(T\).

  • Rising to falling gives \(t_H\approx250\) ms.

  • Falling to rising gives \(t_L\approx750\) ms.

Calculate from the trace

\(T=t_H+t_L=1\,\mathrm{s}\)

\(f=1/T=1\,\mathrm{Hz}\)

\(D=t_H/T\times100\%=25\%\)

Optional analyzer: PWM decoder

Add the PWM decoder; map its Data input to D0 and choose active-high polarity. Compare its duty-cycle annotations with your cursors. These describe the electrical HIGH time; an active-low LED would be on during LOW.

Sources: sigrok PWM decoder; illustrative waveform, nominal delays

docs.title: UART capture: generate a byte you can recognise
Configure the UART analyzer: the settings must match the sender
docs.text:
Add UART; click its decoder row to edit the channel mapping and options.

Decoder field This example TX D0 (GPIO17) RX unassigned Baud rate 115200 Frame: data/parity/stop 8 / none / 1 (8N1) Bit order LSB first Invert TX no Data format ASCII or hex Sample point 50% (default)

There is no clock wire

The decoder uses the baud rate to locate bit centres after the start edge. \(T_{\rm bit}=1/115200\approx8.68\,\text{\textmu s}\). One 8N1 frame has 10 bits: about 86.8 .

Check the result

Expect repeated A or 0x41, without framing errors. Changing the decoder to 9600 does not change the captured wire: it only interprets it incorrectly. The 2 MHz sample rate is not the 115200 baud rate.

Sources: sigrok UART decoder options; illustrative 8N1 frame

docs.title: I2C capture: read a BME280 chip ID
Configure the I2C analyzer: map clock and data
docs.text:
Add the I2C decoder; open its settings and verify the assignments yourself.

@L3.4cmL2.9cm@ **Decoder field** & **This example** SCL & D0: GPIO18 SDA & D1: GPIO19 Displayed slave address format & **shifted**: 7-bit address

No baud-rate field is needed

I2C carries its own clock on SCL. The decoder reads SDA at the clock edges; the capture sample rate still has to resolve both lines.

Why does 0x76 sometimes appear as 0xEC?

  • The wire sends 7 address bits + R/W.

  • Write byte: \((\texttt{0x76}\ll1)|0=\texttt{0xEC}\).

  • Read byte: \((\texttt{0x76}\ll1)|1=\texttt{0xED}\).

  • shifted displays 0x76 plus Write/Read. unshifted displays the raw address byte, 0xEC/0xED.

Inspect the first event

START = SDA falling while SCL is HIGH. A falling SDA edge during SCL LOW is normally a data transition. A simple SDA-edge trigger cannot distinguish them.

Sources: sigrok I2C decoder: channel mapping and address-format options

docs.title: Read the decoded transaction: who sends each part?
docs.text:
Expected BME280 chip-ID read at address 0x76, register 0xD0:

  1. ESP32 writes the register number 0xD0. Sensor ACKs the address and register.

  2. endTransmission(false) keeps the bus for the repeated START before reading.

  3. Sensor sends 0x60: BME280 ID.

ACK is the ninth clock pulse

The receiver drives LOW = ACK or leaves HIGH = NACK. The ESP32 sends NACK after the final read byte to end the read: here it is expected, not an error.

Measure adjacent SCL rising edges inside a byte: \(T_{\rm SCL}\approx10\,\text{\textmu s}\), so \(f_{\rm SCL}\approx100\) kHz. Exclude gaps between bytes.

Sources: Bosch BME280 datasheet; illustrative decoder annotations

docs.title: Capture first, decode second: fix the right setting
docs.text:
@L3.0cmL4.3cmL5.1cm@ **What you see** & **Likely reason** & **What to check/change** Flat trace & wrong probe, pin, GND, or no activity & Inspect the wiring and running sketch; remove the trigger for a first look. Waiting for trigger & chosen edge never occurs & Check the input/edge; arm before the transfer; try a repeating test signal. Pulses, no decoded text & missing channel mapping, too little zoom, or capture begins mid-frame & Open decoder settings; map the inputs; zoom in; capture a complete frame/START. UART garbage / framing errors & wrong baud, frame or inversion & Match 115200, 8N1, LSB first, no inversion; measure $T_{\rm bit}$ to verify baud. I2C NACK on address & wrong address, unpowered device, or wiring & Check 0x76/0x77, pull-ups and SCL/SDA; final read NACK is normal. Edges disappear / timing looks wrong & sample rate too low or window too short & Increase $f_s$ for detail and increase $N_s$ to retain the required time window.

Keep evidence you can explain

Save the capture as .sr and retain the PulseView setup if saved alongside it. Record the probe-to-GPIO mapping, \(f_s\), sample count, trigger and decoder settings. A decoder can be reconfigured on saved data; a missed pulse requires a new capture.

Sources: PulseView manual: decoding, cursors and saved sessions

  2. How many signal wires for 3 SPI devices?

    GND.

docs.title: Why state machines?
docs.text:
Try simulation: State machines

Try simulation: Coffee machine, step by step

  • Real systems have modes: a washing machine is idle, washing, paused, spinning …

  • In each mode the same input means something different: the start button starts, pauses or resumes.

  • A state machine explicitly models the mutually exclusive modes of a system and the events that cause transitions between them.

Benefits

  • easier to read

  • easier to debug (print the state!)

  • easier to expand (add a state)

  • more reliable: impossible combinations cannot happen

Without

Complex programs become a long list of ifs and flags that nobody understands any more.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6
