docs.title: Read a state diagram: states, events and guards
docs.text:
• States: circles, named after what the system is or does.

  • Transitions: arrows labelled with the event (and optional condition / action): event [guard] / action

  • Start: black dot and an arrow to the initial state. It marks where execution begins; it is not a normal event.

  • Specific behaviour per state: what is on, what is checked.

The hardest part

Converting the user story into states. Underline the verbs (“waits”, “heats”, “alarms”) and the events (“button”, “after 5 s”, “too hot”).

Sources: Notation from the temperature-control example Mastering State Diagrams in UML: A Comprehensive Guide, via lecture 5

docs.text:
• tooCold(desiredTemp): event with a parameter.

  • ready / turnOn(): the event triggers an action on the transition.

  • Heating can contain nested states. Its own Start arrow selects Activating when Heating is entered.

An optional final state

A dot inside a circle marks the end of a process. Controllers that keep running may have no final state.

Current state Event Action / next state IDLE stop request do nothing; remain IDLE WASHING stop request pause; go to PAUSED SPINNING stop request stop spinning; go to DRAINING

Safety by design

switch / case
docs.text:
Try simulation: State machines

switch.ino
switch (currentState) {
  case IDLE:
    Serial.println("System idle");
    break;
  case RUNNING:
    Serial.println("System running");
    break;
  case ERROR:
    Serial.println("System error");
    break;
  default:
    Serial.println("INVALID STATE");
    break;
}

Download this example

  • Runs the block that matches the value of one variable.

  • switch: “handle every possible value of this variable”. if: “check whether this particular condition is true”.

  • break ends the case. Without it, execution falls through into the next case!

  • default: all other values.

Only integers and enums

switch works with int, char and enum, not with String or float.

Try simulation: Intersection controller

crossing.ino (part 2)
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) pinMode(PINS[i], OUTPUT);
  pinMode(KEY1, INPUT);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(KEY1), onKey1, RISING);
  enterState(CAR_GREEN);
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long t = millis() - stateStart;    // time in state
  switch (state) {
    case CAR_GREEN:
      if (requested && t >= 5000) enterState(CAR_YELLOW);
      break;
    case CAR_YELLOW: if (t >= 2000) enterState(ALL_RED);   break;
    case ALL_RED:    if (t >= 1000) enterState(PED_GREEN); break;
    case PED_GREEN:
      if (t >= 5000) { requested = false; enterState(ALL_RED_2); }
      break;
    case ALL_RED_2:  if (t >= 1000) enterState(CAR_GREEN); break;
  }
}

Download this example

  • Each case = one state of the diagram: only its transitions (the lights were set on entry).

  • No delay(): the loop runs freely, so the button and anything else stay responsive.

  • Compare the code line by line with the diagram: they must match.

Race condition avoided

The ISR only sets requested; all state changes happen in loop() via enterState().

Why low power matters
docs.text:
• A battery stores charge in mAh: 2000 mAh = 2000 mA for 1 hour, or 1 mA for 2000 hours.

  • Average current decides the lifetime: \(\displaystyle I_{avg} = \frac{I_{on} \cdot t_{on} + I_{sleep} \cdot t_{sleep}}{t_{on} + t_{sleep}}\)

  • Always awake with Wi-Fi (\(\approx\) 100 mA): \(\approx\) 20 hours.

  • Mostly in deep sleep: months to years.

Strategy

  1. Wake up (timer or button).

  2. Measure quickly.

  3. Send the data.

  4. Go back to deep sleep.

Also

Lower the CPU clock (setCpuFrequencyMhz(80)), switch off Wi-Fi when not needed, remove power LEDs on the final hardware.

docs.title: delay() vs millis()
docs.text:
Try simulation: Timers

delay(ms)

  • The program stops for that time: it is blocking.

  • During delay(1000) a button press is simply missed.

  • Fine for tiny examples, a problem in real systems.

millis()

  • Returns the number of milliseconds since start-up (unsigned long).

  • Like a clock on the wall: you look at it and continue working.

  • Wraps to 0 after \(\approx\) 49.7 days (micros(): after 71 minutes).

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Non-blocking timing with millis()
docs.text:
Try simulation: Timers

nonblocking.ino
const int LED_PIN = 2;
const unsigned long PERIOD_MS = 250;
unsigned long lastToggle = 0;
bool ledOn = false;

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
  Serial.begin(115200);
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastToggle >= PERIOD_MS) {  // overflow-safe
    lastToggle = now;
    ledOn = !ledOn;
    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, ledOn);
  }
  // loop stays free for other work: echo serial input
  if (Serial.available()) Serial.write(Serial.read());
}

Download this example

Why?

delay() freezes loop(): buttons, sensors and network are ignored meanwhile.

  • Pattern: “has enough time passed?”

  • now - last >= period works even when millis() wraps after \(\approx\) 49 days.

  • Several independent “timers” in one loop().

docs.text:

  • The whole loop takes microseconds and runs thousands of times per second.

Compare with delay()

A delay(250) would be a box that blocks: during it, the other work never happens.

three_timers.ino
const int LED_BLUE = 23, LED_RED = 21;
unsigned long lastBlue = 0, lastRed = 0, lastPrint = 0;
bool blueOn = false, redOn = false;
void setup() { Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(LED_BLUE, OUTPUT); pinMode(LED_RED, OUTPUT); }
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastBlue >= 300) {          // every 300 ms
    lastBlue = now;
    blueOn = !blueOn;
    digitalWrite(LED_BLUE, blueOn);
  }
  if (now - lastRed >= 1000) {          // every 1 s
    lastRed = now;
    redOn = !redOn;
    digitalWrite(LED_RED, redOn);
  }
  if (now - lastPrint >= 2000) {        // every 2 s
    lastPrint = now;
    Serial.printf("uptime: %lu s\n", now / 1000);
  }
}

Download this example

  • Each job has its own “last time” variable.

  • The jobs do not wait for each other: impossible with delay().

  • loop() runs thousands of times per second and every round asks “is it time?”.

Pattern to memorise

if (now - last >= interval) { last = now; \dots{} }

Sources: Lecture 2: function-specific timers Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Polling vs interrupts
docs.text:
Try simulation: Interrupts

Polling: “has it happened yet?”

  • The program checks the input every round: if (digitalRead(pin)) { \dots{} }

  • Simple, but if loop() is busy the event can be missed or handled late.

  • Like checking the door every minute to see if someone is there.

Interrupt: “handle this now!”

  • The hardware watches the pin and interrupts the CPU when it changes.

  • The CPU pauses loop(), runs a short function (the ISR), and continues.

  • Like a doorbell: you react only when it rings.

Event-driven programming

Interrupts are used for fast or rare events: pulses from a sensor, a button that must never be missed, a timer tick, received data.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: attachInterrupt(): connecting a pin to a function
docs.text:
Try simulation: Interrupts

(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), isrName, mode); (digitalPinToInterrupt(34), buttonISR, RISING);

  • “When pin 34 goes from LOW to HIGH, immediately run buttonISR().”

  • Notice: no parentheses after buttonISR! We pass the address of the function, we do not call it ourselves (&buttonISR means the same).

  • Any GPIO of the ESP32 can trigger an interrupt.

RISING LOW \(\rightarrow\) HIGH FALLING HIGH \(\rightarrow\) LOW CHANGE any edge

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Two button circuits: the same press, opposite edges
docs.text:
Pull-down: active HIGH

  • Released: resistor holds the input LOW.

  • Pressed: contact connects it to 3.3 V, so HIGH.

  • Press = RISING; release = FALLING.

Pull-up: active LOW

  • Released: resistor holds the input HIGH.

  • Pressed: contact connects it to GND, so LOW.

  • Press = FALLING; release = RISING.

NO = normally open

These contacts are open when the button is released. The course board uses the left-hand arrangement: KEY1/KEY2 are active HIGH.

Sources: Course-board schematic; GPIO API Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation

docs.title: Choose the mode from contact type and wiring
docs.text:
Normal means the button is released: NO = open, NC = closed.

@l L3.5cm c c l l@ **Contact** & **Circuit** & **Released** & **Pressed** & **Press** & **Release** NO & pull-down; contact to 3V3 & LOW & HIGH & `RISING` & `FALLING` NO & pull-up; contact to GND & HIGH & LOW & `FALLING` & `RISING` NC & pull-down; contact to 3V3 & HIGH & LOW & `FALLING` & `RISING` NC & pull-up; contact to GND & LOW & HIGH & `RISING` & `FALLING`

Choose in this order

Identify the contact and resistor, determine the released and pressed levels, then select the edge for the event you want. A press does not always mean FALLING.

Momentary versus latching

A momentary push button returns when released. A latching switch holds its new position; interrupt edges still follow the resulting GPIO voltage changes.

docs.title: Read the waveform: press, release or both?
docs.text:
CHANGE detects both edges

An ideal press-and-release cycle produces two events with CHANGE. Holding the button produces no further edges. Contact bounce can produce extra events in any edge mode: choosing RISING or FALLING is not debounce.

docs.title: Configure the input and the interrupt separately
docs.text:
Course board: KEY1 (GPIO34)

course_button_setup.ino
// Configuration fragment: NO button to 3V3,
// external pull-down already on the board.
void setup() {
  pinMode(34, INPUT);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(34),
                  onPress, RISING);
}

Download this example

  • External pull-down: use INPUT. GPIO34/35 have no internal pull resistors.

  • To handle release instead, choose FALLING.

Breadboard: GPIO25 to GND

pullup_button_setup.ino
// Alternative configuration fragment:
// use an internal pull-up on GPIO25.
void setup() {
  pinMode(25, INPUT_PULLUP);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(25),
                  onPress, FALLING);
}

Download this example

  • INPUT_PULLUP: released HIGH; pressing connects the input to GND.

  • To handle release instead, choose RISING.

Two different choices

An external pull-up/down already supplies the bias: use INPUT. INPUT_PULLUP and INPUT_PULLDOWN enable internal resistors; attachInterrupt() selects the edge. These alternative setup fragments assume a short ISR named onPress. Pass its name without parentheses; handle the signalled work in loop().

Sources: GPIO and interrupt configuration Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation; ESP-IDF Programming Guide: GPIO & RTC GPIO (ESP32)

docs.title: What happens when an interrupt fires
docs.text:
Try simulation: Interrupts

  1. The event happens (edge on the pin).

  2. The CPU finishes the current instruction and stops loop().

  3. It saves where it was and runs the ISR (Interrupt Service Routine).

  4. It returns to exactly the next instruction of loop().

Sources: Figure: The Engineering Projects ESP32 Interrupts, via lecture 3

docs.title: Writing a good ISR: volatile and IRAM_ATTR
docs.text:
volatile bool buttonPressed = false; void IRAM_ATTR buttonISR() { buttonPressed = true; } volatile

  • Tells the compiler: this variable can change unexpectedly (in the ISR).

  • Without it, the compiler may keep a copy in a register and loop() never sees the change.

  • Not the same as “volatile memory” (RAM)!

IRAM_ATTR

  • Puts the ISR in internal RAM instead of flash: it can run immediately, even while flash is busy.

  • IRAM is small: only ISRs, not everything.

Keep ISRs short!

  • Other code (and other interrupts) is waiting.

  • Timing of the rest may go wrong.

  • Long ISRs can crash the board (watchdog).

  • No Serial.print(), no delay(): set a flag, do the work in loop().

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; ESP-IDF Programming Guide: GPIO & RTC GPIO (ESP32)

docs.title: Example: a button interrupt on the course board
docs.text:
Try simulation: Interrupts

button_interrupt.ino
const int KEY1 = 34;               // active HIGH
const int LED_GREEN = 22;
volatile bool pressedFlag = false;
volatile uint32_t pressCount = 0;
void IRAM_ATTR onKey1() {
  pressedFlag = true;              // short!
  pressCount++;
}
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(KEY1, INPUT);
  pinMode(LED_GREEN, OUTPUT);
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(KEY1), onKey1, RISING);
}
void loop() {
  if (pressedFlag) {               // handle the event here
    pressedFlag = false;
    digitalWrite(LED_GREEN, !digitalRead(LED_GREEN));
    Serial.printf("presses: %lu\n", (unsigned long) pressCount);
  }
  delay(2000);   // ISR still counts rising edges while loop waits
}

Download this example

  • RISING: the course-board buttons are active HIGH.

  • The ISR only sets a flag and counts.

  • loop() does the slow work (Serial, LED).

  • The counter records rising edges, including bounce, during delay(2000).

Experiment

Press several times during the delay: compare the edge count with the number of LED toggles. The Boolean flag merges events; debounce is still needed.

docs.title: Flowchart: main loop and interrupt
docs.text:
Try simulation: Interrupts

Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

The ISR is a separate, short flowchart started by the hardware. It only sets a flag; the main program does the slow work.

docs.title: Bouncing: one press, many edges
docs.text:
Try simulation: Button debouncing

  • Mechanical contacts bounce for 1–20 ms when pressed or released.

  • An interrupt sees every bounce: one press can count as 3, 5, 10 presses.

  • Hardware fix: RC filter (the course board has 220 pF; often 10 k\(\Omega\) + 100 nF).

  • Software fix: ignore new edges for a short time after an accepted one.

Sources: Figure: electrosome.com, via lecture 3 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Debouncing in software
docs.text:
Try simulation: Button debouncing

In the ISR (time stamp)

debounce_isr.ino
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 50;
volatile unsigned long lastPressTime = 0;
volatile uint32_t presses = 0;
void IRAM_ATTR onKey1() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastPressTime > DEBOUNCE_MS) {
    lastPressTime = now;
    presses++;          // valid press
  }
}

Download this example

Polling (stable for 30 ms)

debounce_poll.ino
const int KEY1 = 34;
int stable = LOW, lastRead = LOW;
unsigned long lastChange = 0;
void loop() {
  int r = digitalRead(KEY1);
  if (r != lastRead) {             // moved
    lastChange = millis();
    lastRead = r;
  }
  if (millis() - lastChange > 30 && r != stable) {
    stable = r;                    // accepted
    if (stable == HIGH) Serial.println("press");
  }
}

Download this example

Choose

ISR version: reacts instantly, ignores bounces after the first edge. Polling version: accepts a new state only after it has been stable for a while.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Arduino Language Reference

docs.text:
Try simulation: Button debouncing

Try simulation: Arduino to flowchart

  • First diamond: did the contact move? Then restart the stopwatch.

  • Second diamond: has it been stable long enough and is it a new state?

  • Only then count the press: the bounces never reach the third diamond.

docs.title: Hardware timers: interrupts from the clock
docs.text:
Try simulation: Timers

  • A timer counts clock ticks, independent of loop().

  • When it reaches an alarm value, it fires an interrupt.

  • Precise periodic events: sample a sensor exactly every 1 ms, generate a signal, a clock tick.

  • The classic ESP32 used in this course has 4 general-purpose 64-bit hardware timers.

@L4.4cm L3.4cm@ **Call** & **Meaning** `hw_timer_t *timer;` & pointer to a timer object `timerBegin(1000000)` & claim a timer, tick frequency in Hz (1 MHz = 1 μs) `timerAttachInterrupt(timer, &onTimer)` & run `onTimer()` at the alarm `timerAlarm(timer, 500000, true, 0)` & alarm at 500 000 ticks, auto-reload, repeat forever (0)

Period

period \(=\) alarm value \(/\) tick frequency \(= 500\,000 / 1\,000\,000 = 0.5\) s

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; Arduino ESP32 Core Documentation; Espressif Timer API: 4 timers on ESP32

docs.title: Core 3.x: timerBegin() allocates an available timer
Prescaler: divide the timer clock, not the CPU clock
docs.text:
Classic ESP32: 4 hardware timers, each with a 64-bit counter and a 16-bit prescaler.

\(f_{\rm tick}=\dfrac{f_{\rm clock}}{P} \qquad T_{\rm tick}=\dfrac{P}{f_{\rm clock}}\)

Arduino-ESP32 core 3.x: timerBegin(1000000) requests a 1 MHz tick rate; the driver selects the clock/divider. Here, an 80 MHz source gives \(P=80\).

The CPU keeps its own clock

The prescaler divides the clock received by the timer peripheral. It does not change the ESP32 CPU frequency.

Sources: Espressif Timer API: timer count, counter and prescaler; classic ESP32, APB-clock example

docs.title: Prescaler trade-off: resolution versus counter range
docs.text:
Same 80 MHz source and same counter width; only the prescaler changes.

\(P\) Tick frequency Time resolution Time to wrap (relative) 8 10 MHz 0.1 \(\mu\)s \(1\times\) 80 1 MHz 1 \(\mu\)s \(10\times\) 800 100 kHz 10 \(\mu\)s \(100\times\)

Small prescaler

Fast counting, short ticks: finer time resolution. The counter reaches its maximum sooner.

Large prescaler

Slow counting, long ticks: coarser time resolution, but a longer interval before the counter reaches its limit.

For a \(B\)-bit up-counter starting at zero: \(\displaystyle T_{\rm wrap}=2^B T_{\rm tick}=\frac{2^B P}{f_{\rm clock}}\).

Wrap is not an alarm: wrap follows the largest counter value (\(2^B-1\)). A configured alarm can trigger and auto-reload much earlier, at \(N\) ticks: \(T_{\rm alarm}=N T_{\rm tick}\). The classic ESP32 counter has \(B=64\).

Sources: Espressif Timer API; calculated examples for an 80 MHz timer clock

docs.title: Ticks, frequency and timer intervals
docs.text:
Info

timerBegin() sets the timer tick frequency, not the CPU clock. If an LED toggles once per alarm, one full blink needs two alarms: \(f_{\rm LED}=f_{\rm alarm}/2=1\,\mathrm{Hz}\) in this example.

Sources: Arduino-ESP32 Timer API (core 3.x)

docs.title: The timer counter: a sawtooth, an alarm and an ISR
docs.text:
\(f_{\rm tick}=2000\,\mathrm{Hz}\); \(N=2000\) ticks

\(T_{\rm alarm}=N/f_{\rm tick}=1\,\mathrm{s}\); \(f_{\rm ISR}=1\,\mathrm{Hz}\).

What happens at the top?

Reaching 2000 triggers the alarm: hardware reloads 0 and requests the ISR. The ISR does not reset the counter. Ramps are simplified; interrupt latency is not drawn.

Open Serial Plotter, 115200 baud. Count climbs once per second; ISR is a short marker printed by the next loop() iteration.

Sources: Arduino-ESP32 Timer API; classic ESP32, core 3.x; illustrative timing

docs.title: timerStop(), timerRestart() and timerStart()
docs.text:
Example: 1 MHz; alarm = 500 000 ticks = 0.5 s of counting after a reset.

@l L9.5cm@ **Call** & **Effect** `timerStop(timer);` & Pause counting; retain the current count and timer configuration. `timerStart(timer);` & Resume from the saved count; it does not reset the counter. `timerRestart(timer);` & Set the count to zero. A stopped timer still needs `timerStart()`.

Start at the right moment

timerBegin() starts counting immediately. To configure before running: begin \(\rightarrow\) stop \(\rightarrow\) configure \(\rightarrow\) restart \(\rightarrow\) start. Paused time does not count towards the next alarm.

Sources: Timer API; Arduino-ESP32 3.3.11 implementation; illustrative timing

docs.title: Hardware timers
Ticker: timers made easy
docs.text:
Try simulation: Timers

ticker.ino
#include <Ticker.h>

Ticker sensorTicker;
Ticker ledTicker;
const int LED_BLUE = 23;
bool ledOn = false;

void blinkLed() {
  ledOn = !ledOn;
  digitalWrite(LED_BLUE, ledOn);
}

void readSensor() {
  Serial.println(analogRead(36));
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(LED_BLUE, OUTPUT);
  ledTicker.attach(0.5, blinkLed);       // every 0.5 s
  sensorTicker.attach_ms(100, readSensor); // every 100 ms
}

void loop() {}       // empty: the tickers do the work

Download this example

  • Ticker is part of the ESP32 core: no installation.

  • attach(seconds, fn), attach_ms(ms, fn): repeat.

  • once(seconds, fn): run once, e.g. a timeout.

  • detach(): stop.

Still keep them short

Ticker callbacks run in a shared timer context: no long delay() inside, or other tickers are delayed.

Sources: Example from lecture 3 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: How precise is time?
docs.text:
• All timing comes from a 40 MHz quartz crystal.

  • A typical crystal has a tolerance of \(\pm\)10–20 ppm (parts per million).

  • \(20 \cdot 10^{-6} \times 86\,400\) s \(\approx\) 1.7 s per day.

  • Prescalers, clock synchronisation and temperature effects: out of scope for this course.

Need real clock time?

Use NTP over Wi-Fi (configTime()) or an external RTC chip (DS3231) instead of counting millis().

millis() vs timer

millis(): good to \(\approx\) 1 ms, depends on how often loop() checks. Hardware timer: μs precise, independent of loop().

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6; ESP32 Series Datasheet

docs.title: Priorities, watchdogs and race conditions
docs.text:
Priorities and watchdogs

  • Several interrupts can be pending: they are handled in order of priority.

  • A watchdog timer checks that the system is still alive and that ISRs are not too long. If not: reset.

  • Message: Interrupt wdt timeout on CPU1 \(\Rightarrow\) your ISR was too long or blocked.

Race conditions

  • The result depends on the timing or order of events that use shared data.

  • Two interrupts update the same variable.

  • A timer event occurs while loop() is changing the state.

  • Hard to find: the bug appears “sometimes”.

Simple rules

Let one side write a shared variable; keep shared variables small (bool, 32-bit); use flags; do all real work in loop().

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Example: a race condition and its fix
docs.text:
Bug: a pulse can be lost

race_bug.ino
volatile uint32_t pulses = 0;
void IRAM_ATTR onPulse() { pulses++; }

void loop() {
  delay(1000);
  Serial.println(pulses);  // ISR may fire...
  pulses = 0;              // ...here: lost!
}

Download this example

Fix: only the ISR writes

race_fixed.ino
volatile uint32_t pulses = 0;
uint32_t lastPulses = 0;
void IRAM_ATTR onPulse() { pulses++; }

void loop() {
  delay(1000);
  uint32_t now = pulses;          // 1 read
  Serial.println(now - lastPulses);
  lastPulses = now;               // our copy
}

Download this example

  • Left: between printing and resetting, an interrupt can increment pulses; the reset erases it.

  • Right: loop() never writes pulses. It reads it once (a 32-bit read is atomic on the ESP32) and works with the difference.

Sources: Race conditions: lecture 6 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Quiz: time and interrupts
docs.text:
1. Why is now - last >= interval better than now >= last + interval?

    Check your answer

    The subtraction keeps working when millis() wraps around after 49.7 days.

  2. What goes wrong if the ISR variable is not volatile?

    Check your answer

    The compiler may cache it: loop() never sees the ISR's change.

  3. attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(34), onKey(), RISING); does not compile. Why?

    Check your answer

    onKey() calls the function; pass its address: onKey.

  4. One press on the button gives 4 counts. Name two fixes.

    Check your answer

    RC filter in hardware; software debounce (ignore edges for \(\approx\) 50 ms).

  5. Timer with timerBegin(1000000) and timerAlarm(timer, 250000, true, 0): frequency?

    Check your answer

    Period 0.25 s \(\Rightarrow\) 4 Hz.

docs.title: What is a variable?
docs.text:
Try simulation: Variables

  • A named place in memory that holds a value your program can read and change.

  • Every variable has four properties:

  • Name: how you refer to it (ledPin)

  • Type: what kind of value and how many bytes (int)

  • Value: what is stored now (2)

  • Address: where in memory it lives

  • The compiler chooses the address; you choose name, type and value.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Variables in memory
docs.text:
Try simulation: Memory layout

  • Memory is a long row of bytes, each with an address.

  • A variable occupies as many bytes as its type needs.

  • The ESP32 stores multi-byte numbers little endian: the lowest byte first.

  • A pointer (int*) is a variable that holds an address: you will meet them in libraries.

Sources: Figure: c-jump.com, via lecture 1 Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Declaring and using variables
docs.text:
Try simulation: Variables

declare.ino
const int ledPin = 2;   // constant: never changes
int counter = 0;        // declared + initialised
int lastValue;          // declared only

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  counter = 10;         // assignment
  counter = counter + 1;
  Serial.println(counter);   // 11
}

void loop() {}

Download this example

  • Declaration: type name; reserves memory.

  • Initialisation: give a first value at the same time.

  • Assignment = copies the value on the right into the variable on the left.

  • const: the compiler refuses any later change. Use it for pin numbers and settings.

Uninitialised local variables

A local variable without a first value contains garbage. Global variables start at 0, but always initialise anyway.

docs.title: Naming rules and conventions
docs.text:
Rules (the compiler checks)

  • Letters, digits and _; no spaces.

  • Must not start with a digit.

  • Case sensitive: ledPin \(\neq\) LedPin.

  • No reserved words: int, if, for, class …

Conventions (humans check)

  • camelCase for variables and functions.

  • UPPER_CASE for constants.

  • Names describe the meaning, not the type.

Bad Good int x = 23; const int LED_BLUE = 23; int t; float temperatureC; int a1, a2; int potRaw, lightRaw; bool f; bool pumpOn; int 2ndValue; int secondValue; int delay; int blinkDelayMs;

does not compile; delay hides the Arduino function.

docs.title: Data types on the ESP32
docs.text:
Try simulation: Variable types

Type Bytes Range Typical use bool 1 true / false flags: pumpOn, buttonPressed char 1 \(-128 \dots 127\) one ASCII character 'A' uint8_t / byte 1 \(0 \dots 255\) raw bytes, I2C data, LED brightness int16_t 2 \(-32\,768 \dots 32\,767\) sensor registers int / int32_t 4 \(\approx \pm 2.1 \cdot 10^{9}\) counters, ADC values, pin numbers unsigned long / uint32_t 4 \(0 \dots 4\,294\,967\,295\) millis(), micros() long long / int64_t 8 \(\approx \pm 9.2 \cdot 10^{18}\) very large counts float 4 \(\approx\) 7 significant digits temperature, voltage double 8 \(\approx\) 15 significant digits precise calculations String varies text messages (uses heap memory)

Same name, different size

On an Arduino Uno an int is only 2 bytes (\(-32\,768 \dots 32\,767\)) and double = float. Code that counts to 100 000 works on the ESP32 but overflows on the Uno. Use int32_t, uint8_t … when the size matters.

docs.title: Binary: how a computer stores numbers
docs.text:
Try simulation: Number representation

  • A bit is 0 or 1: off/on, false/true, no current/current.

  • 8 bits = 1 byte \(\rightarrow\) \(2^8 = 256\) combinations.

  • Each position has a weight: a power of 2.

  • Everything (numbers, text, images, sound) is eventually stored as bits.

  • The ESP32 is a 32-bit processor: it handles data in 32-bit chunks.

Counting in binary

0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111, 1000 … Just like decimal, but you carry at 2 instead of 10.

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Decimal, binary and hexadecimal
docs.text:
Try simulation: Number representation

Dec Bin Hex 0 0000 0 1 0001 1 2 0010 2 7 0111 7 9 1001 9 10 1010 A 11 1011 B 12 1100 C 13 1101 D 14 1110 E 15 1111 F

  • Hexadecimal (base 16) uses 0–9 and A–F.

  • One hex digit = exactly 4 bits (a “nibble”): a byte is always 2 hex digits.

  • That is why datasheets and I2C addresses use hex: 0x76, 0x3C.

The same number, three ways in C++ int a = 60;``int b = 0b00111100;``int c = 0x3C; Converting by grouping 0x3C \(\rightarrow\) 3 = 0011, C = 1100 \(\rightarrow\) \(0011\,1100_2\) \(\rightarrow\) \(32+16+8+4 = 60\)

Leading zero

int x = 012; is octal (= 10), not twelve!

docs.title: Converting decimal to binary: step by step
docs.text:
Try simulation: Number representation

Method: divide by 2, keep the remainders

200 100 rest 0 100 50 rest 0 50 25 rest 0 25 12 rest 1 12 6 rest 0 6 3 rest 0 3 1 rest 1 1 0 rest 1

Read the remainders bottom to top: \(200 = 1100\,1000_2 =\) 0xC8

Check it in the Arduino IDE

bases.ino
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  int x = 200;
  Serial.println(x, BIN);   // 11001000
  Serial.println(x, HEX);   // C8
  Serial.println(x, DEC);   // 200
  Serial.printf("0x%02X\n", x);  // 0xC8
}
void loop() {}

Download this example

Powers of two to remember

1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 (12-bit ADC), 65 536

int b = 2000;
int c;

c = a + b;     // 3000
c = b - a;     // 1000
c = a * 3;     // 3000
c = b / 3;     // 666  (integer!)

int count = 1000;
count = count + 10;   // 1010
count += 10;          // 1020
count++;              // 1021
count--;              // 1020

Operator Meaning + - * / add, subtract, multiply, divide % modulo: remainder of a division += -= *= /= short for x = x + \dots ++ -- add / subtract 1

Modulo is surprisingly useful

n % 2 == 0 \(\rightarrow\) even number i % 4 \(\rightarrow\) counts 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, … (cycle 4 LEDs) seconds % 60 \(\rightarrow\) seconds within the minute

Sources: Embedded Programming, lectures 1–6

docs.title: Integer pitfalls: division and overflow
docs.text:
Try simulation: Variable types

pitfalls.ino
int sum = 10 + 20 + 30;
int avg1 = sum / 4;             // 15: wrong count
int avg2 = sum / 3;             // 20: correct

What is the Arduino Software (IDE)?
docs.text:
The Arduino Integrated Development Environment—or Arduino Software (IDE)—connects to Arduino/ESP boards to upload software and communicate with them. It brings together in a single graphical interface essential tools for software development, such as a code editor, compiler, and debugger.

The programs, also called sketches, are writen in the code editor and save as a .ino file.

docs.title: Download the IDE
docs.text: First things first: Download the Arduino IDE on the official website Arduino.cc.

docs.title: Connect the ESP32 and Install the Driver
docs.text:
To establish a serial connection with your ESP32 device, use a USB-to-UART bridge. This allows your computer to communicate with the ESP32 for programming and debugging.

In some cases, the USB-to-UART bridge is provided as an external module. This approach is common for compact development boards or final products where minimizing space and cost is important.

  • The chip enables bidirectional communication (conversion):
    • from the ESP, it converts UART to USB for the PC.
    • from the PC, it converts USB to UART for the ESP.
  • So what is the purpose of the driver?
    • it allows the operating system to recognize this chip as a virtual serial port (COM).

That is what we will do! ;)

  1. First connect the ESP32 to the PC.
  2. Download and install the CP210x driver: CP210x USB to UART Bridge VCP Drivers.
  3. Check whether the installation was successful. In the Device Manager, under "Ports," the Silicon Labs CP210x USB to UART should appear.

For more details, refer to the ESP32 Serial Connection Guide.

docs.title: IDE at First Glance
docs.text:
When you open the IDE for the first time, this sketch window appears.

  • void setup(): runs only once. Used for initialisations.

  • void loop(): runs in a loop. Statements are executed infinitely.

In summary, this is the basic structure that every Arduino program follows. The setup() function runs once at the start, typically used for initialization, while the loop() function contains the main code that runs repeatedly. This structure ensures your program can continuously respond to inputs and perform tasks.

// this is a comment

void setup()
{
    //this part will be run just once
}

void loop()
{
    //this part will be executed in a loop
    //(as the name of the function suggests)
}

docs.title: Example 1: Hello World
docs.text:
The codes below show two options for printing "Hello World" via Serial communication. Please open the Serial Monitor in the Arduino IDE to see what is being transmitted.

// ESP32 "Hello, world" — v1
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);          // Open serial at 115200 bps
  Serial.println("Hello, world"); 
}

void loop() {
  // Nothing to do here
}

// ESP32 "Hello, world" — v2
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
}

void loop() {
  Serial.println("Hello, world");
  delay(1000);
}

Question: What is the difference in the behavior of the codes?

  • In the first code, "Hello, world" is printed only once, right after the ESP32 starts, because the Serial.println("Hello, world"); command is inside the setup() function, which runs only once.
  • In the second code, "Hello, world" is printed repeatedly every second, because the Serial.println("Hello, world"); command is inside the loop() function, which runs continuously. The delay(1000); causes a 1-second pause between each print.

docs.title: What are digital input and output pins?
docs.text:
• Digital Output: A pin configured as output can send a HIGH (3.3V) or LOW (0V) signal. Then powering an LED for instance. Example: turning an LED on or off.

  • Digital Input: A pin configured as input can read external signals as HIGH or LOW. Example: checking if a button is pressed.

Important to note that in many microcontrollers, every GPIO is at least digital. Some GPIOs have extra capabilities, such as analog input, PWM, or special functions such as connectivity protocols. For the ESP32-WROOM-32, please refer to the "Pin Definitions" chapter in the datasheet.

docs.title: Turning a single LED on and off
docs.text:
// Turn on an LED using ESP32

// Define the pin where the LED is connected
const int ledPin = 23;

void setup() {
  // Initialize the LED pin as an output
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);

  // Turn the LED on
  digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);
}

void loop() {
  // Nothing else to do in the loop since the LED remains on
}
  • const int: Declares the variable (ledPin) as a constant integer.
  • pinMode: Initializes the pin as INPUT or OUTPUT. This allows the pin to send/write voltage to the LED (OUTPUT) or to receive/read (INPUT).
  • digitalWrite: Sets the output of the pin to HIGH or LOW.
Exercise 1 **Task:** Develop a program to light up multiple LEDs. **Solution:** [ex1](ex1/ex1.ino) Exercise 2 **Task:** Develop a program to light up multiple LEDs. Make them blink in sequence (use the `delay()` function). **Solution:** [ex2](ex2/ex2.ino)

docs.title: Input Examples – Buttons
docs.text:
// Reading the state of a button with ESP32

const int buttonPin = 34;  // GPIO where the button is connected
int buttonState = 0; // state of the button

void setup() {
  // Initialize Serial Monitor
  Serial.begin(115200);

  // Configure the button pin as input
  pinMode(buttonPin, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  // Read the state of the button
  buttonState = digitalRead(buttonPin);

  // Print the state
  if (buttonState == HIGH) {
    Serial.println("Button is pressed!");
  } else {
    Serial.println("Button is not pressed.");
  }
}

docs.title: The switch statement
docs.text:
Instead of using many if..else statements, one can use the switch statement. The switch statement selects one of the code blocks to be executed according to an specific condition/expression:

switch (condition_or_expression) {
  case Case1:
    // code block 1
    break;
  case Case2:
    // code block 2
    break;
  case Case3:
    // code block 3
    break;
  default:
    // default code
}

docs.title: Example: Switch statement
docs.text:
int day = 3;

switch (day) {
  case 6:
    printf("Today is Saturday");
    break;
  case 7:
    printf("Today is Sunday");
    break;
  default:
    printf("Weekday! ;)");
}
  • Obs.: break exits the switch. If the command is omitted, the execution falls through into the next case. For more details refer to w3schools.

docs.title: ESP32 hardware timer interrupts
docs.text:
Use an ESP32 hardware timer to toggle an LED at a fixed interval without blocking loop().

Board package

These examples use the Arduino-ESP32 3.x timer API. The classic ESP32 has four general-purpose hardware timers; the available number depends on the ESP32 variant.

docs.title: Frequency, ticks and interval
docs.text:
A timer counts ticks. The frequency determines how many ticks pass each second, and the alarm value determines how many ticks trigger an interrupt:

\[ T_{\mathrm{alarm}} = \frac{N}{f_{\mathrm{tick}}} \]

At 10,000 Hz, an alarm after 20,000 ticks fires every 2 seconds. One tick lasts 100 microseconds. Toggling an LED on every alarm gives a complete on/off cycle every 4 seconds.

docs.title: Configure a hardware timer
docs.text:
hw_timer_t *timer = timerBegin(10000);  // 10,000 ticks per second
timerAttachInterrupt(timer, &onTimer);
timerAlarm(timer, 20000, true, 0);      // repeat every 20,000 ticks

timerBegin() starts the counter after configuration. timerAlarm() enables the alarm. Keep the interrupt handler short; perform printing, lengthy calculations, and other slow work in loop().

void setup() {

  Serial.println("Enter a number and press Enter:");
}

void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() > 0) { // read only when data is waiting
    int value = Serial.parseInt();   // read an integer number from serial
    Serial.print("You entered: ");
    Serial.println(value);

    if (value > 5) {
      Serial.println("The entered value is greater than 5");
    } else if (value < 5) {
      Serial.println("The entered value is less than 5");
    } else {
      Serial.println("The entered value is equal to 5");
    }
    Serial.println("\nEnter another number:");
  }
}
